MY BRAVE LADDIE. Tap, tap, along the pavement,lap. It came, a little crutch. A pale-faced looked up at me. "I do not mind it much," Ile answered to my pitying look. "It might be worse, you know; ' Some fellows have to stay in bed, While I quite fast can go." "Oh, yes, I used to run about, Perhaps I may again; The doctor says it's wonderful I have so little pain; It hurts me now and then, of course,.

Well—ever since Qat fall, But I'm so very glad, you see, That I can walk at all." Tap, tap, the little crutch went on, I saw the golden hair, The brown eyes wide and all aglow, 2: The noble, manly sir; And somehow tears*, moment came, And made my vision dim, While still the kiddie's cheerful words Were sweet as sweetest hymn. I lam so very glad, pm see, That I can walk al all." Why, that's the way for us to feel When troubles may befall. There's always blue sky somewhere, friend, Though clouds around you meet, And patience will the Master send, If sought at Ills dear feet, M. E. SAirosrmi, in Congregtionalist.

Banished from ads own land by, delicacy of health, the poet has, he tells us, been 'Obliged to takemp his permanent abode among the mountains of •Sw4zerland. Hew acutely he feels this forced sacrifice of social ,life is seen in the first pathetic sonnet. It is no wonder if the !blessing of heal is a subject of ;peculiarly deep and pathetic in- terest ton poetdike Mr:Symonds, who has so bitterly learnt its 'value. That youth andthealth sus life's only blessings, life has 'taught him, omit teaches ns all, too late. When in a recent lee- lure Sir -Andrew Clarke defined health as "the skate in which 'existence isv (Welt is a joy; in which it is a delight to see, to hear., to think, atid to be; in which men are able to discharge the duties of tife,,to hear the trials of life, to resist the temptations of • evil, and too on the journey of life getting and giving joy,' he simply describe-id the paradise of youth, which is only fully under- stood when 'Whits become a paradise lost. The poet's tttonghte sas thispoinbace very touching.]

UNCONSCIOUS INFLUENCE.—WO azeeouching our fellow beings on all sides_ They are affected for go+d or for evil by what we eze, by what we aley and do, even by what we think and feel. May flowers in the parlour breathe their fragrance through the atmosphere. We are each of us as silently saturating the atmosphere about us with the subtle aroma of our characters. In the family circle, besides and beyond all the eeiaching, the daily life of each parent and child mysteriously modifies the life of every person in the household. The same process on a wider scale is going on throegla ehe com- munity. No man livetb to himself, and no an dieth to himself. Others are bellt up and straightened by our unconseieus deeds- and earns may be wrenched out of their places and thrown down by our unconscious in- fluence.—Co4yresfationalist. SKEWERS ANP Pnts.--Skewers of wood formed a regu- lar portion of toilette or wardrobe requisites long after the reign of Queen Elizabeth, who herself fastened on her lighter garments not with pins, but with wooden skewers. But it must be borne in mind that Elizabeth had not the enjoyment of several modern appliances. She breakfasted upon salt beef and beer, and her, Royal fingers served her at breakfast and all other meals in lieu of forks, which at that time were unknown in Eng- land. The most comfortable apartments of 'her palace were strewed, not with carpets, but with dead rushes and dried leaves. Her carriage was very inferior to the worst cab in existence, and she presented herself in the streets of London, on days of great processions, mounted on a pillion behind her Lord Chancellor, who rode a Flanders mare. Metal pins were used at a very early period. Bone pins are found in Saxon burrows, and some magnificent specimens of Saxon pins are engraved in the A rcheological A Thum, in the possessioa of Lord Conyngham. One has the stem of brass and the head of gold, ornamented with red and blue stones and filagree-work. Chaucer tells us, in "The Miller's Tale," that when the " joly clerke" Absolon made love to the carpenter's wife, "he sent her pinnes, rnethe, and spiced ale." The constant use of pins is noticed in Heywood's "Four P.'s" and in "The Pinder of Wakefield, 1559." "s!y wench here is an angel to buy pins." Pins with pearls on the head of them are mentioned in VVebster's "White Devil, 1612 ; and pins for the hair in Machin's " Dumb Knight, 1608." ONE TYPE OF NEW ENG/AND WOMEN.—If you Were to enter a small, commonplace, whitewashed farm-house in any of the straggling New England villages, which appears little else than a cluster of huts in a wilderness to English eyes—if you were so bold as to enter in, and so fortunate as to have op uninterrupted conversation with the mistress of the house, you would find her a . plain, probably faded, woman, clad in neat calico, sharp- voiced, and sharp-visaged perhaps, but gentle in man- ner, and displaying as she talks a well-cultivated in- telligence, and more or less familiarity with literature in all its branches of history, philosophy, science, and bell es- ettres. You would find her a member of the nearest library, and a subscriber to all the leading periodicals. i But n order to make this a strictly truthful account, I must add that she seldom reads newspapers, and is utterly devoid of that knowledge of current affairs that distinguishes particularly the women of New York and Chicago. But then, consider how precious to her is each moment of time, and how far is she removed from the centres of life and civilisation! She has no amusements, no diversions, no trips away. nothing but the dull, ever- lasting grind. And yet is she patient, and never resting from her round of necessary duties, and that, to her, no less necessary one of self-culture. Some one has beauti- fully said that " the hand that rocks the cradle is the hand that rocks the world." The children of Priscilla— or, more correctly, "Sairey Ann" will doubtless be rich, and some will call them parvenus, perhaps ; but as for her grandchildren and great-grandchildren, what may they not become !—From Cassell's Family Magazine for January. I guess so!" responded the good man. "I have helped to bring up eight babies." "Are you having much practice now ?" asked an old judge of a young lawyer. "Yes, sir; a great ' deal, thank you." " Ah, I'm glad to hear it, In what line is your practice particularly ?" "Well, sir, particularly in economy." Don't forget three little words—" If you please." Life is made up not of great sacrifices or duties, but of little things, of which smiles and kindness and small obliga- tions, given habitually, are what win and preserve the heart, and secure comfort. High on the desert mountain, full descried, still sits throned the tempter, with his old promise—the kingdoms of this world, and the glory of them. He still calls you to your labour. as Christ to your rest; labour and sorrow, base desires and evil hope.—Ruskin. A NEWWERSION •OF.AN OLD SONCL—Every artist who has illustrated Bobby Busts' song "Comin thro' the Rye" has alway,s mpresenteda maiden wading through a field ' of rye me to her waist, with a stout fellow clasping her ..tarenurd the neck,: preparatory_ to giving her a , hearty • smack. It has always seemed to us that there was a mistake somewhere. Maidens do not usually travel throeglerve-delds. It would trample down the grain, , and inegdotland such cc thing would be severely pun- ished. afiew the thing is explained. There is a small .riveroailcdtheßye in Ayrshire that could be forded most of the season. In-wading over, the lassies have to hold up -their petticoats, and Burns and his rollicking cone panionsased to wait until the lassies were Well into the .stream, Wired they mould rush in and kiss them. The maidens could not resist it, for if they did, they, would , bayed° drop their clothes and get them wet. This is a much more sensible explanation of the song than the one that has obtained credence In society generally. The grain field idea will have to take a back seat. How A PLUM-PUDDING WAS MADE IN PARIS.—Most of our readers have heard of a famous attempt to make a real English plum-pudding in Paris, and how it failed, in spite of all the .art of all the king's cooks, because they were not told to tie the materials in a cloth. Dr. Sehomberg, of Reading, in the early part of his life, spent a:Christmas at Paris with some English friends. They were desirous to celebrate the season, in the man- ner of their own country, by having as one dish at their , table an English plum-pudding but no cook was found equal te the task of oompounding it. A clergyman of the party had, indeed. ea old receipt-book ; but this did , not suffieiently explain the process. Dr. Schomberg, I however, sepplied all that was wanting by throwing the recipe into the form of a prescription, and sending it to the apothecary to be ,made up. To prevent all possi- bility of errsr, he directed that it should be boiled in a cloth, and seat in the same cloth, to be supplied at an hour specified. At this hour it arrived, borne by the apothecary's assistant, and preceded by the apothecary himself, dressed according to the professional formality of the time, with a sword. Seeing when he entered the apartment, instead of signs of sickness, a table well. filled and surrounded by very merry faces, he perceived that he was made a party in a jeke that turned on him- self, and indignantly laid his hand on his sword; but an invitation to taste his own cookery appeased him, and all was well. DIFFUSION OF FOLK STORIES.—With regard (1) to the origin of the peculiar and irrational features of myth and merchen, we believe them to be derived and inherited from the savage state of man, from :the savage condi- tions of life, and the savage way of regarding the world. (2) As to the diffusion of the tales, we think it impos- sible at present to determine how far they have been 'transmitted from people to people, and wafted from pluamcetoce i o n the obscure and immeasurable past of an antiquity, how far they may be due to identity of human fancy everywhere. (3) As to the relations between "Household Tales" said Greek or other civilised myths, we prefer the following theory, which leaves room for many exceptions. The essence both of vuirchen and myths is number of impossible and very peculiar in- cidents. These incidents are due to the natural qualities of the savage imagination. Again, the incidents are .combined into various romantic arrangements, each of these arrangements being a marches. The nizirchen were originally told, among untutored peoples, about anony- mous lyeroes—a boy, a girl, a lion, a bear—such were the leading characters of the earliest tales. As tribes became settled, these old stories became localised, the adventures (originally anonymous) were attributed to real or imaginary named persons or gods, and were finally edomed by the fancy of poets like the early singers of Greece. Thus, while a savage race has its mdrchen (in which the characters are usually beasts or anonymous persons), the civilised .race (or the race in a state of higher barbarism) has the same tale, developed and elaborated into a localised myth, with heroes rejoic- ing in such noble names as Perseus, Odysseus, Jason, Leminkainen, or Maui. But while the progressive classes in civilised countries are acquainted with the . named heroes and elaborate forms of the legends, the comparatively stationary and uneducated classes of shepherds, husbandmen, woodmen, and fishers retain a ' version but little advanced from the old savage story. They have not purified away the old ferocious and ir- rational elements of the tale, or at most they have sub- stituted for the nameless heroes, characters derived from history or from Christian records. Thus the "House- hold Tales" of the European peasantry occupy a mean position between the savage story, as we find it among African tribes, and the elaborate myth which, according to our theory, poets and priests have evolved out of the original savage data.—From "Grimm's Household Tales," with notes (80/i's Edition).

THE FATAL -BOAT ACCIDENT AT QUEENSFERRY.—The Flintshire Assizes opened at Mold on Monday, before Mr. Justice Stephen. There was only one case for trial, viz, that of John Peter Davies, 56, agent to the River Due Com- pany, charged with mans'aughter in connection with the accident at Queens.ferry on Dec. 20, by which three lives were lost. His Lordship, addressing the jury, referred to the law regarding manslaughter, and remarked that it was a very' proper and natural feeling, and ohe which he was very far from blaming or not sympathising with, that somebody ought to suffer for such an accident, but be could not see on what ground prisoner could be convicted of manslaughter. The prisoner was discharged. • LINSEED LOZENGES, solidified linseed tea, laxative and de- mulcent, 6d ; postage 2d. Kay Bros., Stockport, and an Chemist ..-41dre.

all for want of the proverbial stitch in time. A proper instrumeat shed, with sparred gates, and with its floor raised a little to be free from damp, is a very necessary buikling." It should have a large roomy press placed near thesdoor, where small things liable to lose could be locketimp. The tool-house is of equal importance. It I should be situated for convexiienteccess, should be dry, ' and ;if it contains a fireplace so much the better. Snowed the walls plenty of pins and shelves should be fixed, on which to hang and lay small articles. Ploughs aragenerally kept in repair by the local blacksmith per contract; but, in addition, the farmer would do well to have them thoroughly Creaned,tthe mould 'boards greased, and the rest of the plough painted or black var- mished. Grubbers, too, st some convenient time during ,summer, should be cleaned, repaired, and painted, or tarred; and harrows should be repaired after they are not neeeed, and should be painted and put away. Sow- ing machines for corn are far more delicately constructed and need better treatment. They should be carefully Cleaned and repaired, and any little necessary improve- ment made. The coulters of the drill machine should be well cleaned and greased, and all the other parts rubbed with a cloth slightly oiled, and the woodwork painted once every three years. Reaping machines demand the greatest attention to have everything about them right, or very much time is lost, and many people kept idle. It is an excellent plan to have them repaired thoroughly whenever harvest was completed—cleaned, and oiled, and put away into a dry place. Duplicates of all [parts likely to be needed should be kept on hand; and it is a good plan to give half-a-crown extra to each of the two men in charge of the machine during harvest, provided they kept the maehine clean and well oiled, and had everything ready to Start the moment yoking time arrived. Farm engines and mills are generally in charge of the steward. The engine-boiler should be kept clean, and the flues cleaned at least once a year, and any bricks that are broken replaced. • The packing of the cylinder piston or pump renewed as required. The thrashing- machine should also be carefully swept down after being used, and the oil-holes all cleared, and a wet day , chosen for an extra cleaning. Leather belts should be washed in tepid water, and next day oiled with coarse castor oil, which rats will not touch. Straw and hay'. cutters, and any other machine attached to engine, should have similar attention. The knives of hay-cutters require to be kept sharp, and so set as to almost rub against the cutting face. Hard fanners are frequently in a dirty state from too much oil being used. The moving parts should be well cleaned and 'moderately oiled, and this will render them much easier driven. Forks, hoes, and all hand implements should be kept clean and oiled. By so doing, they will be founel to work much easier and last longer, and all axes andilaws should be kept sharp. The foregoing remarks may ap- pear trifling and unnecessary to many farmers; but, for all that, we holddfaat judicious attention to such details saves money.

WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL A meeting of this Council for the purpose of transacting business left over from previous meetings was held in the 'Town Hall on Tuesday afternoon. There were present the Mayor (Alderman liarrison), Aldermen Holmes, Pickmere, Chandley, Kean ; Councillors Broadbent, Brown, Roberts, Mackie, Sutton, Marsh, Bolton, Wright; Messrs. Brooke (town clerk), Whittle (deputy town clerk), Longdin (ear. veyor), and Chorley (borough treasurer).

FINANCE COMMITTEE. . Alderman HOLMES moved the adoption of the minutes of the Finance Committee, one of the minutes being a recom- mendation that the Town Clerk give the necessary notices for the repayment of the following mortgages, and that the same be re-issued to the mortgagees at the reduced rate of interest of XS Ws per cent, per annum as from and after the let July, 1885, upon application to the borough treasurer on or before Ist March next. Notice had been given, Alderman Holmes said, to pay off bonds to the value of £30,000, the whole of which had been re-issued at the reduced interest of £3lOO per cent. This reduced rate would cause a reduction of borough expenditure to the extent of £2OO a year. (Hear, hear.) Notice was also given to pay off another £2olooo.—Alderman PICHMERE : And that will affect a farther reduction.—Alderman HOLmES Yes —Councillor Elnown having seconded the minutes, they were con- firmed.

; PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE. The minutes of this committee contained the following recommendations, viz :—Recommendation, that the tender of Messrs. Darbishires and Co. of Penmaentnawr, for 400 tons of 4in. granite cubes, at 22s 61 per ton, delivered at railway stations, be accepted. Recommendation, that the tender of Messrs. John Nunnerley and Co., Limited, for 400 tons of burr stone, at 3s 8d par ton, delivered in Queen- street, and the tender of Mr. John Lunt for 400 tons of burr stone, at Si Bd, delivered In Queen-street, be accepted. Recommendation, that the tender of Messrs. John Nunnerley and Co., Limited, for 25,000 chequered tiles, at 93s 6d per 1,000, delivered at the Corporation Yard, Arpley, and the tender of Messrs. Clare and Ridgway far 15,000 tiles, at 741 2d per 1,000, delivered in Corporation Yard, Arpley, be accepted. _ _
Alderman KEAN moved the adoption of these minutes. Councillor BROWN seconded.

Councillor BROADBENT asked if the Paving and Sewer- age Committee would take up the., consideration of the stag of the road between Warrington and Latch- ford. He had no doubt that the Mayor felt, as he did himself, rather an objection to appealing specially to the Committee to pay attention to any road thtt they used themselves. There might seem a sort of want of pub- lic spirit or selfishness about it, but be had been spoken to by such numbers of persons as to what they said was the very disgraceful state of that road that he really felt quite compelled to say something on the subject. The fact of the road being now used by the omnibuses seemed to necessitate more than ever before that the road should be kept in better order. He did not know whether the Corn- tnittee would think it dvisible to put down white sets or not. Alderman FICEMERE : Pave it with wood. _

Councillor ROBERTS said that-sMina—tiWe—a.go he mentioned whet he thought would be a very judicious thing to ba done; that was the omission of prices at which tenders had been accepted. It was within the power of any ratepayers to get that information if he wanted it, as both the town clerk and the borough surveyor were most willing to give it. There was therefore no detriment to the public In the non-publica- tion of these prices, and he had thought it would be some advantage to contractors if the prices were not published. The Mews thought the prices were never published in the papal?:

COuivoillor Roman: Oh, yes, they are. Cotancillor SUTTON remarked that questions as to the prices were sure to be asked by 1301218 member of the Council, and then the answers would/be reported and go forth to the public. L.
* Council/or ROBERTS said he did not care about pressing the matter.

Councillor MACKIE said the question of special prices Wile one he cared nothing about, but he thought it ought always to be stated if there was more than one tender. If this were done he thought the ratepayees would be satisfied even if they did not kuow the exact shillings and pence.

Mr. 'Burroli said contracts were always advertised. Councillor MACKIE said that was not always the case although there had been a great improvement in that res- pect this last year or two. Alderman normERE said that everybody in town who tender knew about them. _ _

The MAYOR said he fully concurred with the observations made by Mr Broadbent. He thought those who had driven over the road to Latchford knew what an intensely disagree- able operation it was. It was almost enough to dislocate one's spine, and sometimes it was productive of the feeling of general uncomfortableness and irritability. He only wished that something could be dene at once to put the road in a better condition, but he supposed the severe frost they had recently had and the subsequent thaw would have a tendency to break up the roads. Councillor BROADBENT thought the effects of the frost had not been seen yet, and probably the roads would be worse afterwards.. The minutes were then confirmed. A MYSTRRIOVS SPECIMEN.

The Museum, Library, and Arts Committee recommen- ded that a loge specimen of stibnite, an ore of antimony from Mount Kosang, Japan, be purchased. Councillor MACKIE moved the confirmation of these minutes. Councillor Simms seconded.

Alderman PICKMERE said he was not very learned in geology and he should like to know what was meant by the above minute, whether somebody wee to go to Japan to purchase the specimen--(Council- tor BROADBENT : "And who is to go," and laughter)--and what was the money to be expended upon it. Coun. MACKIE thought they might take it for granted that the Museum Committee had done very properly in ordering that specimen, although his own necessary absenc3 from their meetings left him unable to give an explanation. In a town like Warrington they had so much to do of a snechanical nature that there ought to be everything that could be utilised by their working population. If under the present circumstances the gallant Major would with. hold his curiosity he (Councillor Mackie) promised that a proper answer would be given next Tuesday. (Laughter.) Alderman PICKMERE said he found the committee was as dark on the subject as he was himself. Mr. BOLTON wanted to know the reason of this pur- chase.

The MAYOR explained that two or three specimens were brorzght before the committee, and they agreed to purchase them at the price of three guineas. It was considered by the committee a very desirable thing to have. Alderman PICHMERE : We will say nothing more about it.

Councillor Surrox : I have no doubt if it were going to ooet 2d somebody would want to know something about it. Councillor BOLTON: SO we ought to do. (Laughter.) The minutes were confirmed. THE CEMETERY COMMITTEE. Councillor Bitows moved, and Alderman KEAN seconded, the adoption of the minutes of the Cemetery Committee.— The M&YOR said he was sorry to mention that the chair- man of this committee (Alderman Thewlis)., had been ex- ceedingly unwell during the last two or three days, but he was happy to sty he was now very much improved, and hopes were entertained that they should again see him at that Council. (Hear, hear.) Councillor BROADBENT said a very large increase in the death rate was shown on the minutes. Sixty-two adults had been interred, as compared with 43 in the corresponding period of last year, and 106 minors, as 'compared with 54. Perhaps the mover of the minutes had something to say on the subject. Councillor Hamm did not think he was in a position to give a satisfactory account why there should be that ap- parent increase. Councillor BROADBENT: It is not merely apparent, but real. Councillor BROWN said it was more apparent than real. But they had certainly had a large amount of measles and other sources of disease, and although the increase was more in appearance than reality, still the death rate had been more during the last month than in the corresponding month of last year, which was, however, below the average. Upon the whole he did not think the deaths were much in excess of the average. The MAYOR thought the questions as to the death rate came more within the scope of the duties of the Sanitary Committee. He also mentioned that there had been more than 100 deaths from 'measles during the past six months.
The minutes were confirmed. _ THE MARKETS COMMITTEE. _ _

The minutes of this committee contained the following : Application received from the Warrington Cocoa Company, Limited, for further accommodation in the market; resolution that the Company be allowed to occupy the premises now used as the office of the market inspector, at the rent of £4O per annum, increased from £36. Alderman CHANDLEY moved, and the MAYOR seconded the a loption of these minutes. Councillor MACKIE said he should like to express the earnest hope that the projected extensions of the Market Committee which were more or leas. before the public should not include any further extension of the half-crown- a-day shops. He hoped that without the special considera- tion or permission of the Town Council nothing of that kind was brewing, and when the matter came on next Tuesday evening he should expect to get some definite information about it. In the meantime he entered his protest against anything being done in that direction. Alderman CHANDLEY hoped that Councillor Mackie or any other member of the committee having anything to say as to the action of the Market Committee would put it in some tangible form and give some reason for their action. He pad not expected to hear anything more about that matter, but nevertheless they should be very happy to do so._
The minutes were confirmed. THE OAS.

Alderman HoLmEs moved and Councillor WRIGHT seconded, the confirmation of the Gas Committee's mi.entes. Coun. BROADBENT asked for some information as to the quality of the gas. Unless, he said, one-half or three- quarters of the people of Warrington were very much mis- taken,there was a very general impression which he shared that the gas was very impure and very dirty. The gas made a room smell where it was burnt, and produced a great deal of smoke.

Alderman HOLMES said that the committee had never heard anything about the smelling of the gas. They had had some complaints as to the lighting power of the gas, but that had arisen perhaps because there was not sufficient pressure at the works to drive it so as to produce more illuminating power in gentlemen's private houses. He would inquire whether the officials at the gas works had heard any of these complaints, for up to the present the committee had not had any before them. The minutes were then passed. GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE. The minutes of this committee contained the following : Resolution : That a memorial be forwarded to the Post- master-General to establish a snb-post office, with money order and telegraphic departments, at the east side of the borough, in or near Church-street. Resolution : That the Borough Surveyor be instructed to go to Chester and Pres- ton to inspect and report upon the maps deposited with the Clerks of the Peace, showing the proposed divisions under the Redistribution of Seats Bill.—ln answer to the Mayor, the BOROUGH SURVEYOR said he had been to Chester and Preston, and found that there was nothing on the map to affect Warrington.—Minutes conSirmed.

INVITATION TO THE CIRCI79. The MAYOR. said he had a communication of great impor- tance from Mr. W. B. Harmston, the proprietor of the Circus. It read as follows:—" I shall feel extremely grate- ful and pleased if you will kindly honour my entertainment with your patronage and presence one evening convenient to you all. I havean excellent company, good stud of horses and my performanc s are refined and of a high-class nature' I may mention that on a previous visit to this town I had. the honour of the patronage of the Mayor and Corporation one evening. I hope you will honour me on this occasion with your patronage and presence, and I can assure you nothing shall be wanting on my part to give you a very enjoyable evening." Alderman PICKMBRE : Is that to the Mayor and Corpora- Lien?
The MAYOR said it was addressed to the Mayor, aldermen, and_councillom.

Mr. BOLTON said a member of the Council wanted to know if there were free tickets. (Laughter.) Alderman PICKIdERB: Because if that is so Mr. Bolton will support it. (Laughter.) The MAYOR said Mr. Harmston had certainly been very liberal in his contributions to local charities, and he (the Mayor) should be very happy to invite them all to tea on that evening, and also to g) to the Circus at his expense if they .would.
Thisinvitation of the Mayor was unanimously accepted, and it was agreed that a suitable evening for visiting the Circus should be fixed.

COrNTED OUT. The Council was then proceeding to the consideration of the bye-laws when Alderman Holmes and Councillor Bolton left the roam, the latter in doing so calling attention to the fact that there was not a quorum present. The meeting consequently ctme to an end.

LYMM LIBERAL ASSOCIATION. The annual business meeting of this Association was he.d in the Mission-room, Lymm, on Monday evening, when there was a good attendance. Mr. Swanwick presided, and remarked that they were met under new and invigorating circumstances, different to any under which Liberals had ever before met together in Lymrn. When one considered all that had happened since the meeting held on the 3rd November last at the Plough it fairly took away one's breath. They could not but admire the infinite tact and zeal that was exercised to bring about the extraordinary and speedy result that had been witnessed. Having expressed that ad- miration, the next thing was to heartily congratulate and welcome those who were new going to be electors and who had so long looked forward to the privilege which at this time next year would he theirs. They believed that the ac- cession of the new electors to the right that had so long been denied them would be an immense advantage to the electors themselves, and a still greater one to the country at large. lithe old electors had to congratulate the new ones, they had also to congratulate themselves, because they would now have a far more vigorous, healthy, and lively state of politics in that neighbourhood than they had had before. The change there and in other similar districts throughout the country would be enormous. They were now not only face to face with a new and entirely altered condition of political matters in their district, but were face to face with a large amount of work. Ile was sure that the earnestness of their meeting that ceening would be the beginning of every hard- working year, and he trusted that each work would ter- minate ins great and glorious success. (Applause.) They had ascertained pretty closely what the number of electors in Lymm township alone would be, that was to say, cutting off Warburton and Thelwall on the one side, and various places on the other side. In Lymm township alone they had hitherto had under 300 electors, and now they would have 800. (Cheers) They would require to make their organisation thorough and effective in order to carry the Liberal candidate at the next election. When the new Par- liament—from which so much would be expected—met, a number of important changes would be forced upon the country that would require their consideration, and they would still have work to do. They should require the help of all Liberals, not only on the polling day, but at many other times. Questions connected with the land and county government would come forward, questions the work and revolution regarding which would occupy them for many years to come These subjects touched them so nearly that they would have to attach themselves heartily to them as an asseciation and as individuals. What be was especially anxious for was that throughout the neighbourhood they should work solidly together, that they should recognise one another's rights and claims, giving way as much as possible to each other's claims, and not presenting sharp corners to to each other. There was one question it would be interest- ing to have settled. That was, their own position under the Redistribution Bill. They did not yet know where they were going to be. They were asked , for by three separate divisione of Cheshire. The Commissioners put them in Daresbury division. In the Altrincharn division the line was drawn at the Jolly Thresher, 80 that they were near the edge, and the Knuts- ford division took in part of High Legh. If the Commis- sioners' scheme was adopted, Lymm would go with War- rington. Latchford, Runcorn, and Northwioh, but they would have seen from the reports of the meetiag at Chester that there was a strong agitation in the salt districts to be grouped by themselves. If that was done it must so much modify the scheme that it was extremely probable that Lymm would be thro on in either with the Knutsferd or Altrinctham districts. They must possess themselves with patience until Parliament met, and they saw what was the final decision of the Commissioners. They were certain to have a contest next year, for it had been decided that every division of Cheshire should be contested. Therefore the neceselty for work remained the same, whatpver district they were attached to. At any rate, the township of Lymm would not be divided, and their work would have to be the same wherever they went. He then proposed the first reso- lution, expressing the opinion of the meeting that the limity of disfranchisement of boroughs should be 20,000 of popu- lation, instead of 15,000; supporting the amendment to the first and seoond schedules of which Mr. Arthur Arnold, M.P., was given notice, to include in the former those boroughs which have a population less than 20,000, and to include in the latter the Universities of Oxford, Cambridge, • and Dublin. He cordially agreed with the resolution, thinking that that mode of adding 12 members for Scotland without increasing the total number of members was a very good one.—Mr. Brewtnall seconded the resolution. Him- self, he should be glad to see the number at which borozghs should have a member put a little higher still. (Hear, hear) As regarded the Universities mentioned, he should be glad to see them deprived of a privilege which he thought they had not mood themselves worthy of retaining. (Hear, hear.) He did not think they had any more reactionary parties to deal with than those three Universities. It seemed like a Blur upon education in its highest form that such a charge should be made, but unfortunately it was true.— Mr. Watson supported the resolution, and remarked that he did not see why members of the Universities should have double votes while others had single ones.—Mr. Welford thought it rather invidious to mention the three Universi- ties and not extend the resolution to them all, He objected to the principle of University votes, and should like to see University constituencies straightway abolished—the aboli- tion to extend to Scotland and the London University. He suggested that the resolution should be amended to read " that all the Universities of England, Scotland, and Ire- land should be disfranchised, and that the members so ob- tained should be elected to populous parts of the country and to Scotland."—The suggestion was adopted, and the resolution carried in its amended form.—A second resolution approving of the sub-division of the large constituencies into districts returning one member each, and urging that pressure should be brought to bear upon the Government to induce it to apply that principle universally, and to sub- divide inte one member districts the 23 I::oroughs which are left in the enjoyment of dual representation, was unani- mously passed, as was also a third resolution providing that where a Parliamentary borough was divided into divisions a person should not be entitled to vote in more than one sub- division, the meeting being also in favour that the rule should apply to the division of counties. The Chairman, Mr Watson, Mr Dutton, and Mr Woodford spoke to these resolutions.—lt was decided on the motion of the Chair- man, seconded by Mr .T Holt, that the general committee consist of the members then present, with power to add to their number.—lt was also agreed that the working commit- tee consist of 24 chosen members, the general secretary, and an election secretary, with power to add.—Mr G B Dew burst, of Oughtrington Hall, was elected president for the ensuing year, on the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Mr Dutton.—Mr Thomas Davies was re-elected general secretary and thanked for his past services, and Mr Shil- ling was requested to act as election secretary.—Mr Swan- wick was appointed treasurer on the motion of Mr Dutton, seconded by Mr Brewtnall, and eight gentlemen were ap- pointed to represent the district on the council of the Mid- Cheshire Liberal Association.—This was all the business.

DAIRY Facrc Auxs.-Mr. James Lotig, of Graveley Manor, Hitchir a, delivered a lecture on. " Dairy Farming in the Future' • before the Framlingkam Farmers' Club. He strongly i• *commended dairy factories, and the result of a discuss' itm which ensued was the passing of a reso- lution ram* *rang the committee of the club to take such action as n !my appear to them desirable with a view to the forma' ism of a.dairy factory in Framlingham. DESERY SID COMBENSATION.-.-A Devonshire farm la- bourer w as on Monday awarded 20 guineas by a judge of the E netsar County Court, as compensation for being impriso *ea for three days, at the instance of Mr. Mons- son, of , lfleak House, Sichnouth. The labourer was 70 years 06. age. A dog was straying about on an estate, and a ,earnaer waagoing to shoot the animal. The olcgman save ti the dog's -life. Seeing the name of Morrison un the "caller, he got some one to write to Mr. Morrison. The ;natter asked the labourer to meet him, and then gave hi] stiletto custody. He was locked up for three days on a charge of stealing the dog, and then brought before ti managistrates and dismissed, as there was no pretence 4 ear any suggestions of dishonesty against the old man. ' Flae judge said he had been treated in a monstrous man- ner, and gave judgment for 20. guineas and costs. . RAILWAY RATES.-The crippling of agriculture and , commerce by high rates on the carriage of goods is an evil which demands the greatest attention/ Hundreds of thousands of tons of farm produce that might be pro- fitably carried by the companies at reasonable rates are kept from being sent to our large towns by the exorbi- tant charges made. :If foreign produce can be carried cheaply, why not home produce. A ton of corn coming from abroad could be taken from the Victoria Docks to Peterborough, 76 miles, for es...Bd, including barging and ' every charge; while the -ordinary charge from London for the same distance for English corn would be 14s. sd. American meat is brought from Liverpool to London for 255. a ton, while English meat is charged 50s. a ton. Potatoes from Cherbourg to London are charged 30s. a ton, while the rate for potatoes between Penzance and London is 455. a ton. Fruit is brought from Flushing at the same rate as is charged to bring it- from Sitting- bourne. American cheese is brought from Liverpool to Locadonlor 255. a ton, while Cheshire-cheese, picked up on the way, is charged 425. ,a ton. Olin MEAT SUPPLY.-Sir J. W. Pease, Bart., M.P., read a good paper before the Cleveland Chamber of Agricul- ture, on Friday, on "Our 'Meat Supply." He gave a large number of valuable statistics, and summed up as fellows :-"You may, in conclusion, ask me what is my deduction from all the figures whichil have laid before you. I would answer this question very briefly-that the fortunes of British meat_groWer are very closely wrapped no with those of the meat consumer. The British workman, with good wages in;his pocket, would, at this moment, raise the price of meat by an increased demand, and tax the energies of the world to feed him. Whilst trade is as dull as at present,u.nd wages are low, his consumption is smaller:and meat prices recede. It seems to me that the English farmer has little to fear from the foreigii meat competition, taken as a whole. The Australian importation of mutton may become larger, and there are signs that this will: be the case. Judging from Messrs. Read and Pall's most exhaustive report, much increase has not to be expected from some of our sources of supply ; from others there seems a ten- dency to send us less. 11: This testimony is due to the decrease in weight of the foreign animal. The American and Continental working classes are even worse off than our own and are not consuming, the same quantities as they would were they better paid. Therefore looking at the position of the English farmer as the great purveyor of meat, I would say that if by wise and careful regula- tions we uan stamp out disease arising at home and pre- vent its importation abroad, that if we have fair seasons, and if the trading interests have a fair demand for their productions, then, in my humble opinioe, the English farmer hes little to fear from foreign competition. The market will beat-his door. THE PR.ICH OF WHEAT, IN 1884.-The fluctuation in the weekly average price of wheat has been greater during the past year than in 1883, but not so much as in 1882, in which it was 12s. id., whereas inlBB3 it was 4s. 10d., and in 1884 Bs. 7d. a quarter. The annual average for the past year was considerably lower than in 1883. In the latter year it was 41.5. 7d., whereas in 1884 it has been 355. Bd.-adall of ss. 11d. a quarter. Taking the two past years *2.883 and 1884, the annual average has fallen 9s. 5d under 1882. The annual average price of corn per bushel was-wheat, 4s. 51.; barley, 3s. 10d ;. oats, 2s. 6d. It may be remarked thatthe average price of barley for 'five weeks in 1884-viz., from November 15th to December 13th-exceeded that of wheat. On November 29th last wheat was 30s. sd. and barley:3ls. 3d., being 10d. a quarter above wheat. ' Barley as-gene- rally about 12s. a quarter below wheat; in fact, taking the past M years, barley has averaged 13s. 6d. below wheat. The two Saturdays that have already passed this year have exhibited a rise in the price of wheat- viz., January 3rd, 31s. Ils., and Januar), 10th, 325. 7d. This rise, with that since November 29th last, when it was 30s. 5d., equals 2s. 2d. a quarter. This may be cheering to farmers, but it will be well to build no great expectations on a rise during such a short period. Nevertheless, as wheat generally rises and falls every four years, it may be the commencement of an upward movement. On looking over a diagram showing the an- nual price of wheat for 243 years-viz., from 1641, we see that wheat has not been so low for upwards of a cen- tury. It is curious to note that in 1780 the annual aver- age price was exactly the same as in 1884-355. Ad. Previous to 1780, a period of 139 years, wheat was 52 years under this average and 87 years above it.-Times. ENSILAGE AND MILE.-Efforts are being made to throw discredit on the ensilage system by calling in question the high quality of the milk produced by cows fed on silage. The attack can be easily refuted by those who have had any experience in feeding dairy cows on silage. In the first place, all ensilaged products vary in nutri- tive quality and general character quite as much as hay does./ The latter substance, if made from the mowings of a peat morass, would be far different from the best clover or meadow grass hay. Just in the same way i would silage differ n accordance with the character of the original material- from which it was mule which alone shows the extreme folly of any sweeping con-, demnation of ensilaged products generally. But Mr. Gibson, the owner of an extensive dairy herd at Saffron Walden, has abandoned very much the growth of man- gold wurzel for dairy cows, because he finds their milk when fed on silage so much better, and Mr. E. T. Blunt, of Blaby Hall, Leicestershire, after keeping some COWS entirely on silage and others on hay and roots, gives as the result of his experience that, while the quantities yielded by the two lots are about similar, the ensilage-fed cows keep themselves much better, in condition and yield from 4 to 5 per cent, more cream in their milk, winch latter appears to be quite as rich as that yielded by grass-fed cows in summer. He adds, "To my surprise I found the percentage of cream in the milk of ensilage-fed cows was higher than that from the milk of cows fed upon hay, roots, flour, and cake." Mr. George Barham, manager of the Express Dairy Company, states that milk to the extent of 400,0001b5. daily passes under his observation coming from nearly all parts of the kingdom, and some from Holland, and that, so far from the milli of ensilage-fed cows being objectionable to his customers, some of them have asked "to be specially supplied with it because of vtairlahre has observes: been its superior quality." On the winter feeding of dairy einocialltivdisnguccmaulenntgofolc4 heoitwhser cabbage, and turnips. I have no hesitation in saying silage will produce milk of better quality and Savour than either."

MIS 9, 0111t2Rop AND SPA/2120W StAcorrrsat—The fol- lowing letter from Miss Ormerod has appeared in The Times :--" May I ask the favour of being permitted to correct an erroneous and hurtful misrepresentation of my views as to the prevention of bird ravages on crops, which is being widely circulated, without any authority from me, in the journals. After communication with regard to ravages on wheat crops, occurring year after year in certain districts of England, and estimated by the judges of the farm crops in some districts to amount to one-third of the crop, I have thought it right to ad- vise that the number of sparrows which cause this loss should be lessened. I have not taken this measure until after more than a year's careful consideration of the subject in communication with leading agriculturists and ornithologists, and after the corroboration of these views from State entomological observations in my hands from the United States of America. Some of these extend over a long period of time, even as much as 12 years in one locality, and give every requisite de- tail, on which I have founded my advice. I consider it of great importance to check this yearly increasing loss; and though no one can regret more than myself to destroy any animal, I believe in this case (but only in this case) it is necessary just as much as with rats and mice at corn stacks. It is not being done wholesale, as far as I have anything to do with it, but, on the con- trary, I have most carefully pointed out the risk of dis- order arising at present, and likewise after the Ist of March until August no wild birds' can be destroyed without the authority of the owner or occupier of the ground, under the provisions of the Wild Birds' Protec- tion Act, to which I constantly draw the attention of my inquirers. With regard to wholesale destruction' of small birds, I beg most emphatically to deny that. I ever advised anything (If the kind, and my views on this head are given clearly in my report on injurious in- sects for 1883. If bird presence is lowered below the regular average where they are constantly present, the crops would suffer, greatly. I do most assuredly not advise a 'destruction of birds: In the case of the spar- row, the birds congregate in autumn and go out in flocks to the corn land, and it appears to me on the highest ground far better to save the bread of the people than to let it be partly eaten, partly thrown to the ground, by these birds."

Pnufnwo BUSH FRUIT TRERS.—Red and white Our- rants require all the suckers removing, unless.alvaca.ncy has occurred in consequence of a branch dying off. ,It may also be an advantage now and thentto remove a ibranch that has become naked and destitute of fruit ibuds. All this should be taken WO consideration be- fore removing the suckers. All young shoots, or the growth of the past year, must be cut to within two or three buds of the base, or two or three eyes above the clusters of fruit buds. The leader of each main shoot , may be left from three to six inches7ong. according to I their length at the time, as the ;object in view is the I good shape of the Izee. Young trees need the leaders to be left nearly a foot long till they attain the desired height. The number of shoots left for main branches should not be mere than a dozen at any time. The Gooselterry requires all the young growths that are re- tained to be left their entire length, excepting an occa- sional unbsually long one which extends too far, or any portions that appear weakly. It is necessary to remove more old wood from the gooseberry than the currant in order to make room for new growth. All the growth of the past year that it is desirable to remove should be cut close to its starting point, for if two or three eyes are left they produce so many shoots, which crowd each other as the season advances. When we commence to prune a gooseberry tree we first look for barren and ugly pieces, as well as those which have a tendency to grow inwards or to cross each other. The next step will be to reduce the number of the pastZrear's growth till they are about six or eight inches distant at the nearest point. The shoots left should point outwards, and those nearest the centre of the tree should be further:apart Where birds are troublesome to the buds, pruning should be deferred till later in the season, so that if they should strip some of the branches they might be removed and a selection made from the best. As soon as there are in- dications of the birds interfering, it is a good plan to stretch some black cotton in various directions over the trees. This the birds do not always see, and if they come in contact with it in their rapid flight they become scared, and will be shy for a time. A mixture of lime and soot dashed on the trees when wet will prevent the birds devouring the buds SO long as it remains on. , Heavy rains will wash it off, and another apphcation should be made. If any cuttings are required they should be secured before pruning commences and tied in bunches, and half buried in the soil to preserve them from shrivelling, till there is an opportunity to make 'them and lay them in properly. Any young trees in- tended for transplanting should be left unpruned till the , operation is performed and the trees have started to grow. Before the principles of vegetable physiology were so well understood as they are now, many gardeners made a practice of pruning any small- fruit trees they had occasion to plant, in the same manner as established trees. Some of the trees scarcely grew at all, others broke so feebly that in two years' time they were not so large as when first planted. TER PROST GARDEN.—THR GRASS PLOT.—After a spell of frost, when the thaw comes the grads :plot will be very soft. To bring it to its normal- state, there is nothing better than rolling, or beating with the back of the spade, at the same time preventing traffic on it for a few days. Grass is much damaged by being walked on in frosty weather. The blades are stiff, and the pressure of the feet crushes everyone that may be trod upon, and as soon as it thaws every footmark will be quite: black. There are times, however, when the grass has been so dry as not to be influenced by the frost. , THE WlNDOW.—Veronica Blue Gem is a half-hardy dwaf evergreen shrub, scarcely exceeding the height of some of the geraniums. The colour of the flowers is pale blue. They are borne in numerous spikes during late utumn and the winter months. The plant is as well utside at all times, excepting during frosty weather. Ye have only recently become acquainted with it, and from its behaviour so far we feel sure it will make an excellent window plant, and will thrive in any good loamy soil, with a little leaf mould or decayed manure. It cannot be over-watered neither winter nor summer, and during the latter season it may be plunged in ashes in the yard, or in the soil of the garden. In each case it should be provided with the sunniest position.

THE VOLUNTEERS.—The statistical returns or the Tolun-

teer forces of Great Britain, just issued, show that during last year the total strength of the auxiliary services was raised from 209,000 to 214,000, the largest number recorded since the movement commenced, Of this huge total 208,000 are returned as efficient, or 97 per cent of the whole. Lan- cashire returns more than 26.000 efficients, and is second only to Middlesex, which has 26, 300. CHILD MURDER—Mrs. Thompson, wife of a railway por- ter at Colchester, was chopping wood on Monday, when her .baby, five months old, began to cry. She fetched it down- stairs and cut its head open with the hatchet. Afterwards she pot the child to bed and went to bed herself, telling her husband when he returned the child was ill. The doctor when fetched pronounced it dead. The woman has been peculiar for some time.—Remanded.

AN; THE RAILWAY BILLS —Mr. Chamberlain officially contradicts the statement which has appeared in a London contemporary to the effect that he has agreed to support the second reading of the railway bills. The right hon. gentleman says he has come to no decision whatever. That statement had caused much commotion in commercial circles, where it is generally agreed that the effect of the bills would be to increase rail- way rates.

div.p: THE BOUNDARY COMMISSION IN
SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE.

On Saturday, the flop. T. H. W. Pelham held an inquiry at the Sessions House, Liverpool, for the purpose of hearing any objections to the constitution of the several divisions of South-West Lancashire, and of receiving proposals for their alteration. Notice having been given that any person might attend and be heard with reference to the matter, there was a large attendance of gentlemen repzesenting the various divisions of South-West Lancashire. The follow- ing gentlemen were present from Widnes and the district : —Messrs. Holbrook Gaskell, sen , J.P. F. H. Gossage, J.P., E. K. Muspratt, J.P., J. L. Muspratt, J.P., E. Carey, Hol- brook Gaskell, jun., J.P., J. T. Allen (clerk to the Local Board), Rd. Lewis, B. Btown, Jos. Morrison, S. K. Muspratt, T. Handley, H. B. Shore (Liberal agent), J. Johnson Brown (Prescot), and W. Tyler (Prescot). In opening the inquiry, the Commissioner said he had the honour to appear that day to hold the last inquiry as re- garded the county of Lancaster, and also the last inquiry as to the counties of England ; and he need hardly say that this division was by no means the easiest that the Commissioners had had to deal with. It was proposed by the Redistribution Bill to divide South-West Lancashire into seven Parliamentary divisions, and in forming those divisions the Commissioners were to quired by their instruc- tions to have regard to certain considerations. The first division was that of Southport, with a population of 57.643. and would consist of the petty sessional division of South. port, 14 720 ; the municipal borough of Southport,32,2o6 ; township of Thornton, 275; Great Crosby, 9,273; Little Crosby, 553; and Ince Blundell, 316. The division of Ormskirk would consist of Knowsley, C:oxteth Park, and Prescot. with a population of 5,546; Kirkby, 1,041; Ain- tree, 1,437 ; Upholland, 4,435 ; Netherton, 386 •, Sefton, 382 ; Litherland, 7,208; Orrell, 673; and Lunt, 104, mak- ing a total of 54,997. The Bootle division wonld consist of Bootle-cum-Linacre, 27,374; Walton-on-the-Hill, 18,715; Fazakerlay, 533; Wavertree, 11,097 ; Childwall, 187 West Derby (part outside Liverpool city), 33,435 ; Toxteth Park, 10,368; and the city of L'verpool, 552,508. From these there was deducted for the purpovs of computing population, the borough of Liverpool, 605,723, and that gave a total of 48,491 for the division. The Widnes divi- sion would consist of Garston, 10,271 ; Allerton. 830 ; Mach Woolton, 4,541 ; Little Woolton, 1,150 ; Halewood, 1,857 ; Speke, 513 ; Hale, 571 ; and the petty sessional division of Prescot, 34,209, making a total of 53,951. The INewton division would have a population of 51,201, and consist of Culcheth, 2,267: Ashion-in-Makerlield, 9.824 ; 2,219 ; the petty sessional division of St. Heleus, and part of the borough of Warrington. The Ince division would have a population of 53,851, and include Haigh. 1,186 ; Ince, 16,007 ; Pemberton, 13,752; Hindley, 14,715; Orrell, 4,290; Winstanley, 545 ; Blllinge Chapel End, 1 935 ; Billings Higher End, 1,402; and part of the muni- cipal borough of Wigan. The Leigh division would have a population of 52,187, and consist of Atherton, 12,602 Tyldesley, 9,954; Astley, 2,669 • Pennington, 6640; West Leigh, 7,848; Bedford, 7,245; Aram, 2,638; Kenyon, 233; and Lowton, 2,357. As regarded the freehold voters inside the boroughs, in estimating the population it was impossible to lay down any rule. The number of voters in South-West 1 Lancashire at present having such qualifications inside boroughs was 3,715. Mr. Thomas Brocklebank, representing the South-West Lancashire Liberal Association said that body held a fairly attended meeting, when the feeling was that the scheme I propounded by the Boundary Commissioners was a good one taken upon the whole. The meeting accepted the scheme of the Commissioners so far as the divisions of Leigh, Ices, Ormskirk, Southport, Newton, anel Widnes were concerned. With regard to the division of Bootle they came to no conclusion, because the people of Bootle seemed to be so earnest in their opposition N the scheme: The dissentients at the meeting and their grounds of objection were :—Newton: Mr. Charles Pilkington objected to the townships of Billinge, Chapel-end, Billings Higher-end, and Winstanlev, cutting off the collie 7 district of Ashton and Haydock from the colliery district of Rainford and Skelmersdale, preventing the fermation of a large mining constituency.—Rainhill : Mr. Rawlins contended that Rain- hill be included in Widnes. This was supported by Mr. Aspinall, miners' agent, of Skelmersdale.—Orm ikirk : Mr E. Erownhill objected to the urban township of Litherland, ' Orrell, and Ford being included in Ormskirk.—Southport Mr. Clark and Mr. Morris objected to the inclusion of Great , and Little Crosbies, Thornton, and Ince Blundell in the division of Southport. As Southport is increasing so rapidly, they consider the petty sessional division should be taken as the division, the remainder going to Ormskirk.— Bootle : The Mayor (Alderman Leslie) objected that the district proposed by the Commissioners was unworkable, and no part of it beyond Walton had any community of in- terest with Bootle. He proposed that Bootle, part of Wal- ton. Litherland, Orrell, and Ford, a compact district on the Mersey shore, whose interests and pursuits are identical, should be formed into a Parliamentary borough, Fez ikerley and West Derby goisg to Ordiskirk, Wavet tree and Child- wall going to Widnes. The Commissioner: The meeting passed everything ex- cept Bootle ?—Mr. Johnson: I'e.—Mr. Edwin Smith re- marked that the Walton people agreed with the scheme put forward by Bootle, and were quite prepared to go along with them.—The Commissioner: I am glad to „find somebody ready to go with them. (Laughter.) Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, as a representative of the Liberal Association, of which Mr. Brocklsbauk was chairman, and being likewise there as connected with Widnes, was deputed to say that they expressed their hearty and cordial approval of the scheme of the Commissioners. It was suggested that as far as Bootle was concerned, the Commissioners should be recommended to take their representations into their se- rious consideration. With these exceptions the Liberal Association very heartily accepted and approved of the Com- missioners' scheme.

Mr. John Johnson Brown, on behalf of the Liberals and Conservatives of Prescot, said be had been instructed to ask the Commissioner to alter the scheme, so that Prescot, which was at the head of Prescot Union, a compact area, should form a township. The Commissioner: With the object of giving the name to Prescot ? Mr. Brown: We do not care so much about Preecot having the name as to its being dissected. They had met the difficulty by making a scheme for the whole of South- West Lancashire. (Laughter.) The speaker was proceed- ing to talk about fancy franchise, when he was stopped by the Commissioner, who said be could not listen to him. Mr. Leresche (Manchester) appealed in support of a memorial from the Corporation of Wigan, but the Com- missioner declined to hear him, declaring that tbe purpose of the application was ta secure two members for Wigan, and that was a matter which he had no power to deal with. The names of Leigh, Newton, and Wigan were agreed to. Mr. Taylor, barrister, opposed the name of Ince, and sug- gested that Hindley would be better. Mr. Ellis (Ince Local Board) said there were figures which would show the way in which Ince had inoreased and the way in which Hindley had been, comparatively speak- ing, standing still. Sir Thomas Edwards-Moss, alluding to the name of Wid- nes proposed to be given to that division, remarked on the character of the manufactures carried on there. He said it was the home of alkali—(laughter)--and the manufactures there were a great nuisance, for, as they knew, no shrub or flower could live within miles of Widnes.
Mr. H. Gaskell : What aboat my place, where flowera grow? _

- Sir Thomas, continuing, said in fact they might say it was a place " where wealth accumulates and leaves decay." (Laughter.) The name of Garston, he thought, was a more proper one and he might say that when down at Garston the other day he saw more vitality than he had seen in any cptarter of Liverpool daring the last six months. Mr. Gossage, chairman of the Widnes Local Board, said he was sorry to see the time of the court taken up with so much frivolity on the part of the last speaker. He handed in a memorial from the Local Board in support of the divi- sion and name as arranged by the Commissioners. Widnes represented 40 per cent of the houses and 46 per cent of the whale population of the division. Garstan was almost de- pendent upon Widnes for its traffic. There was no opposition to the names of Ormskirk and Southport. Sir Thomas Edwards Moss proposed, arra Alderman Les lie seconded, a vote of thanks to the Commissioner for his kindness and courtesy in the conducted that inquiry, Mr. Pelham, in returning thanks, said the objections and suggestions would receive the consideration of the Co.nmis- sinners, and they would endeavour, as far as possible, to see whether alterations could be made to carry out the views of those interested.
FRIGHTFUL DYNAMITE OUTRAGES,
ATTEMPT TO DESTROY THE TOWER AND IHE HOUSES OF PARLIAMENT.

Mr. E. K. Muspratt, on behalf of Widnes, objected to Wavertree and Childwail being added to that division. He might say that both political parties in Widnes entirely concurred in the Comindostoners' scheme. He objected to the Bootle proposal becaus3 it would increase the popu- lation of the Widnes division from 53,000 to 50,000. The Commissioner : That is not very high. Mr. Muspratt said the Widnes population was increasing as fast as that of Bootle, and if the scheme was altered it would be doing an injustice to that town. A series of explosions, believed obi the authority of scientific witnesses to have been caused by dynamite. oc- curred on Saturday at Westminster and the Tower of Lon- don. The plans of the conspirators, all of whom. it is feared, have escaped, Were apparently laid with considerable care, the intention being to completely wreck, if not to utterly destroy, Westminster Hall, the House of Commons, and the Tower of London simultaneously. WESTMINSTER HALL.

Shortly after two o'clock a police constable named Cole was informed by a lady that a bundle was lying in the Crypt below. The c nastable found whit appeirad to be a portien of a lady's Princess robe :oiled round something heavy.' He removed the parcel, and carried it so far as the Hall, when he suddenly heard what an informant describes as a "hazing, whirring sound," and he felt the sensation of heat to his hand. Alarmed, the policeman threw the bundle down at the feet of a gentleman named Green, and at- tempted to make his escape. Almost immediately after- wards there was a terrific explosion. A policeman on duty at the lobby doors says the effect was wonderful. The Hall became suddenly darkened, there was a rattle and fall of several thousands of feet of glass on the stones below, and amidst the darkness and confusion there were shrieks of terrified visitors, and the groans of persons as if in pain. The sound of the explosion was ter- rific from all parts of the House. There was a rush of people, anxious and frightened, when the darkness cleared —a darkness caused by the dust and soot of centuries on the rafters of the hall. It was at once guessed that an in- fernal machine had exploded, spending its force first down- wards, tearing up a large hole in the stone floor, into which Mr. Green had been hurled ; and lying on the floor, mutilated, unconscious, and bleeding, were two police constables—Constable Cole, who brought the explosive from the Crypt; and Constable Cox. who was on duty in the vicinity. Both men were unconscious, and were at once conveyed to the hospital singularly enough, Mr Green escaped with but comparatively little injury. Some workmen engaged close to the iron gate leading to the Crypt in painticg a large model of proposed additions to the Hall, where the Common Law Courts formerly stood, felt the full force of the explosion, and their escape was almost miraculous. The destructive wave passed through the Hall, overthrowing some of the statues, and completely shattering every pane of glass running the whole length of the Hall. The floor of the Hall was literally covered with broken glass and dust and soot to an extraordinary extent. A closer inspection of the scene lea to the discovery that the large iron gates and rails enclosing the Crypt were violently twisted and thrown down, and that considerable damage was done to the masonry facing the steps. The woodwork was shattered and splintered, but the destructive wave travelled through the building in a northerly direction. which accounts for the comparatively small damage thine to the magnificent south window and to the slight sensation felt by the police constable guarding the door leading to the , Houses of Lords and Commons. .

_ The superficial search made as soon as the first sensations of terror were over revealed nothing of the actual character of the machine employed. On the rails were found a few pieces of the woman's dress in which the explosivelvas concealed, and portions of a elk hat, but no detonator or percussion caps or the pieces of clockwork with which the public are now unhappily too familiar.
SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE-MAP OF PROPOSED ELECTORAL PIVISIONS.

For a short time the Hall was a scene of the greatest ex- citement. It is computed that several hundreds of persons were in different parts of the House, and they naturally rushed pell-mell towards the Hall. For a time something like panic prevailed, which was intensified by a second .rio- lent report of an explosion within the House of Commons itself. Then there was a resh from that, no one knowing what to expect and from which quarter danger might be looked for. Within the short space of three minutes, two formidable explosions had taken plane in a building carPfially guarded, and people were anzdous to escaps from a place apparently doomed to destruction. With one exception, the gates of Palace Yard were closed, and there, as well as at each entraace to the Houses of Parliament, a strong force of police was statio ed to keep back the crowds of anxious sightseers who thronged tc, the place from every part of London as well as from many of the neighbouring country districts. In Westminster Diner- ally, and along Whltehall,.the traffic and commotion were exceptionally large, such as is seldom equalled on a popular holiday, but the many thousands of persons excluded, from the precincts of Parliament had to content themselves with such a slight and imperfect impression of the havoc as mild be gathered from peering through the outer railings 0. Palace Yard. In many chtsches and chapels special reference was made on Sunday, in, prayers and sermons, to the alarming and destructive occurrences of Saturday. Sir E. J. Reel, M.P., who was among.the visitors to Westminster, telegraphed in the afternoon to Cardiff that the damage done is very ex- tensive and will take months to repair. It has, however, been arranged that the damage done within th 3 Howe of Commons will, without much delay, be temporarily repaired by way of preparation for the meeting of Parliament on the 19th February:___

Iday, that at the Tower of London may fairly claim•pace- deuce for audacity of conception and recklessness in c---ecu— tion. Hemethere is a strong force of police always on duty, a contingent of Beefeaters- continually on the alert, mad,a. soldiers' guard ever at the Tower gates. The perpetraors of this outrage must thus have run the gauntlet of detiao• tion from each branch of the oervice, and they must have been well aware that if the emplesiota occurred, or if the in.• fernal machine was discovered before they were clear, of the Tema, drawbridge, their chances of escape would; be slight. Saturday one of three days of the week on which visitors are admitted free to inspect the ancient national fortress, ata, this privilege whiott is an innovation of re- cent years, is- cne taken advantage of by a large number i of persons.

The fearf-al explosion, which seemed to shake the massive structure just at two o'clock in the afternoon, caused the most isitense- excitement throughout the citadel. But dis- cipline in the course of a moment or two asserted itself. The troop, were called out and placed under arms' the Tower gstss were promptly closed, and no one allowed either ingress or egress. Sent:its were rapidly stationed at every consiyable point, and the leading officials of the Tower proceeded to the scene of the explosion. This was Ascertained to be in the White 'lower, a capacious round structure, which was. erected in the reign of Wil- liam the Conqueror, and one of the oldest portions of the Tower.

The explosive seems to ha-as been deposited in the south end of the Banqueting Room, which is now used as an Armoury. No explosives are kept in this place by the authorities' and it was speedily apparent that a serious at- tempt had been made to wreck the historic pile. In the meantime the visitors in the Tower were all marshalled and closely examined, with a view to discover the miscreant if possible. The first care was devoted to the wounded, of whom there were many, but only four sustained injuries of such. a character as to necessitate their removal to the hospital. Two of these were young boys, whose wounds caused the blood to flow freely. They were driven oft in a bur- wheeled cab, and their poor little suffering faces caused the liveliest commiseration among the vast crowd which sur- rounded the Tower gates. would it have fared with that dynarnitard had he fallen into the bands of the people then almost frenzied as they were with excitement at the iliabolical cruelty shown by the desperadoes. After the removal of the wounded the examination of these in the tower was proceeded with. Many were in a state of panic, and others half fainting from fright, but before the scrutiny could be commenced another danger threatened. A fire broke out among the wreckage caused by the explosion, and every effort was then directed to ex- tinguish the II Imes. Fire engines were summoned, and with that rapidity which distinguishes the Metropolitan brigade were almost immediately at work upon the ruins. All fears of fire becoming serious were soon at an end, but still the firemen continued to play Amon the ruins for a full hour.

The Beefeaters, under the trying circumstances, did the duty demanded of them nobly, whether it was among the scorching ruins coping with the flames, searching odd cor- ners for other possibly secreted infernal machines, or in dealing with the panic-stricken people. The crowd outside the 'rower were in a ferment of excitement, and it needed all the tact of the police to keep them from forcing their way into the Tower, where they imagined the desperadoes were in safe custody. Later on, however, the detained visitors who had succeeded in satisfying the searching inquiries of the officials, were allowed to depart, and each, one passing out through the gates was at once subject to a running fire of questions from those witho_ut as to what hid really occurred. After a time their excitement subsided but that the excitement within the Tower was a close and trying ordeal for the unfortunate visitors, may be judged by the fact that even at five o'clock, three hours after the ex- plosion, the investigation into the antecedents of some had not concluded, and they were still under detention. The result of Col. Mijendie's examination satisfied him that dynamite was the explosive employed, and that the quantity used was about four or live pounds. He points out that, if properly compressed, this weight of dynamite would only occupy a space ef tour or five cubic inches, and, therefore, there would be little difficulty in arranging it in a package which would go into an ordinary greatcoat pocket, or which could be carried without trouble in the folds of a woman's drew!.

Assistant-Commissioner-General Thorne makes no secret of his belief that it was a woman who was entrusted with the task of depositing the infernal machine. Even suppos- ing the parcel to have been arranged in the most compact and portable form, it would give a bulky appearance to a man's pocket which could hardly have escaped the vigilance of the extra officials on duty in consequence of kindred outrages, whereas a woman's dress would offer much less chance of detection. In connection with this theory it is I stated that some time since it was believed by the police that a woman who has been constantly passing between this country and America was engaged in bringing dyna- mite across the Atlantic, and that the explosive was on each occasion secreted underneath her dress. She was followed without her knowledge on more than one occasion, but, un- fortunately, sufficient evidence couid not be adduced to prove that the suspicions of the police were correct. Preaching on Sunday at St Margaret's, Westminster, Archdeacon Farrar made special reference to the outrage. The attempts of these men, he said, were one of the most frightful signs of the times, in their aimless malignity and in the brutality of the hatred which they exhibited towards England, who desired with all her heart to be just and generous to their country.—Special thanksgiving for pre- servation from danger was offered MI behalf of Inspector Denning and the constables who were on duty at Westmin- ster at the time of the explosion. Archdeacon Farrar, who was in the vestry of St Margaret's Church when the explosion occurred, was an immediate spectator of the I havoc created, and hence the strong feeling he displayed on the subject. In the course of Sunday evening Sir E. Henderson, Chief Commissioner of Police, received the following telegram from Sir Henry Ponsonby at Osborne on behalf of her Majesty :—"The Queen ha e commanded me to ask you as to the condition of the injured policemen." A reply was sent stating that both Cole and Cox were progressing favourably. Photographs of the debris in the Tower were taken on Monday morning, and a search made to reveal the nature of the Infernal machine employed. It is believed that a time-
