div.head: ROUSE OF COMMONS LOBBY.
div.p: ROUSE OF COMMONS LOBBY.

The scare in the lobby of the House of Commms, and in the Hines itself, at ten minutes past two o'clock was one of utter confusion and desolition, and had the explosion taken place here first it is fearful to contemplate what the conse- quence would have been, for it is computed that in the lob- bies and in the house itself there were not less than 200 or 300 persons. Alarmed by the first explosion, they had hastened to quit the building.and fortunately so, or the loss of life must inevitably have been very great. Here the con- spiraMrs had selec'ed a spot admirably calculated to cause the greatest amount of damage with the least expenditure of explosive agency. But intimate acquaintance with the arrangements and internal structure of the House is evident from the very business-like and cold-blooded way in which the details of the plans were prepared and carried out. As habitues of House of Commons know, directly under the Peers and Natinguished Strangers' Galleries, popularly known as " under the clock," are the division lobbies, the Government lobby being to the left on entering the big doors, and the Opposition on the right. In a niche of this 'lobby, where the spice is naturally confined, the dynamit ard carefully placed an infernal machine of sufficient power utterly to wreck the chamber. Could it have been possible for the criminal to have car- ried out this fell design when Parliamait was sitting, and on a night when there was a full House, the dark designs of the moot irreconcilable foe to the British House of Commons would have been fulfilled without stint or measure. At the moment of the explosion, recorded by the stopping of a lobby clock at 2-13, provielentially there was not a single person either in the lobby or in the House. The House and the precincts were deserted even by the officials, who had rushed towards Westminster Hall. _ _

The th ‘r of the members' lobby was thickly covered with glass, and the division lobby itself was perfectly unrecog- nisable. Stout 04it frames were shivered into splinters, and lay in heaps amongst the debris. The tesselatel pavement, which had been torn up, was scattered about in all direc- tions. The downward force of the explosion was again evidenced by the tearing up of a hole in the ground leading to the ventilating apparatus under the floor of the House itself. The whole partition dividing the lobby from the House was carried away bodily, along with all the benches on which Mr. Bradlaugh is accustomed to sit. The wave of disturbance, as usually happens, was very partial and eccentric in its motion, and spent most of its force on the Government side of the House. The Radical benches, being nearest the origin of the explosion, antlered most ; then, passing over the Whig benches' the destructive smoke signalled out the front Government bench, and completely stripped the seat in the centre, which is the Premier's' and thence it impinged on the Speaker's chair, tearing a large hole in the seat, and pirtially splintering the framework. I The current, seemed to travel both inwards and outwards, I the violent concussion completely smashing the glass 1 windows. Everywhere, one trod on the glass strewn thickly on the floor. The lobby clock, over the big doors, had its hands twisted off, but otherwise was uninjured; whilst a small clock to the left, though stopped, was quite uninjured. A more complete wreck, apart from absolute destruction, it Is almost impossible to conceive than the House of Commons after the explosion. The temporary alarm having passed, great anxiety was shown by the officials to ascertain whether there were other infernal machines charged with destruction hidden in the building. As a precautionary measure Mr. Prim, the engineer, ordered the gas throughout the building to be turned off at the meters, and rumour was current that a third machine was hidden behind the Speaker's chair, but this turned out to he incorrect. The officials would not hive been surprised at any discovery after the events of the afternoon, and a complete search of the building was ordered. Intelligence of the atrocity had in the meantime spread far and near, and within half an hour of the occurrence Col. Majendie and Col. Ford (exploeive department) were on the scene, and in company with Col. Sir W. Henderson made a hasty examination of Westminster Hall and the House of Commons. Asked whether he was able to say from the smell pervading the building what explosive was employed, Colonel Majendie replied, •• I was here in time to see the vapour, but not to distinguish the smell. I can tell you what the explosive was not. It was not gtinpowder. It might have been nitro-glycerine,or some compound of nitro- glycerine, probably dynamite." §ir William Harcourt, who was in town, came early and gave imperative instructions to allow no one to enter the building except a member of Parliament or someone intro- duced by a member of Parliament. Lord George Hamil- ton, Mr. Caringten, Mr. Childers, Sir Erskine May, Mr. Edwards, Lord Carrington, Sir James McGarel Hogg, and Mr. Puleston were early _on the _scene.

On inquiry on Monday it was stated that both the injured constables, Cole and Cox, had passed the night satisfac• torily, and their condition is deemed rather more faoourable,. although neither of them is out of danger. Cole's case continues to give the greatest cause of anxiety, but it is possible that both constables may recover. Special precautions are being taken at all the Govern- ment offices, and the doorkeepers are instructed to ex- amine the contents of parcels brought into the courts, if necessary, in order to satisfy themselves as to their nature. Mr. Shaw-Lefevre, the First Commissioner of Public Works, has, it is understood, stated that the damage inflicted on Westminster Hall, the House of Commons, and the Tower cannot be covered by less than £lO,OOO, and that it may possibly extend to £14,000 and even more. A PRISONER AT BOW-STREET. The man arrested at the Tower on Saturday afternoon was brought up at Bow-street on Monday, before Sir James Ingham, the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate. He gave the name of James Gilbert Cunningham. He was a young man, apparently about 22 or 23years of age, of middle height and spare built. He was clean shaved and of an unattractive type of features, high cheek bones, over-hanging upper lip, and sallow complexion. He was dressed in a dark overcoat and felt hat, lie was brought into court in charge of Chief Superintendent Williams and a posse of detectives. He watched the proceedings with great attention, biting his lips from time to time as he leaned forward the better to hear ti-e evidence, and glancing about furtively. No formal charge was read out, but it was stated that the prisoner was charged with being concerned in causing the explosion at the Tower.

Police-Inspector Aberline said that he went to the Tower on Saturday afternaon at 2-40. He found the gates locked, and a number of persons detained there. He was instructed, with other officers, to take the names and addresses and on- ' cupatitras of all persons, and saw them writ,en down. Amongst the persons there was the prisoner, who gave the name of James George Gilbert, and said be lived in a street which sounded like Sherbert-street. Asked where that was, he stated that it was in Whitechapel. Witness then asked him what part of Whitechapel the street w..s in, and he said near Great Alice-street. An inspector who was present at the time asked the prisoner if he did not me in Scar- borough-street, and he said Yu, that is the name of it." After some pressing, he said that he was a labmrer. Sir James Ingloana : Did he say what kind of labour?

Witness : ekedA Min where he had been employed re- cently, and be said" Nowhere." Then I asked him what countryman he was, and after some hesitation he said, " I am an Englishman," and he was last employed at the docks at Liverpool. He further stated that he had lacien in Lon- don for a week, and came to better himself. He then said that he was working in Liverpool for two or three months. He said he had resided at 30, Great Preston-street, White- chapel, where he was known by the name of Gilbert, and that he had removed from there to 32, Scarborough-street. He said he hact been in Amerita for five years, and had come over in a vessel called the Asiatic, where be passed by the name of Cunningham. Witness was directed to ac- company the prisoner to his lodgings, and he there pointed out a black box and brown leather bag as his property. They were taken possession of by the police. He was then taken to Leman-street police office. Shortly after he arrived there a telegram was received Irons Liverpool, and he told the pri • soner that it stated that no such person as Gilbert appeared to be known at the addresses be had given. He subse- quently had a conversation with the prisoner with reference to a brown box. Sir James Ingham asked tha prisoner if he had any questions to put to the withers. The prisoner (speaking with a half Irish and half Yankee accent) : No; but I hive one rem irk to make. He says when he asked me questions I muttered over the re- plies. I did not. I expressed the words as quick as he asked me. Chief Inspector Williamson then asked for a remand.

Sir Jame a Ingham said he must hax, some proof tha, something was dine at the Tower before granting that ac- quest. Witness was then further examined, and said he saw signs of an explosion at the Te.ver, and there had also been fire, on which the engines had thrown a great quantity of water. On passing into the Da' nqueting _Zoom, now teed as an armoury, he found the place in great confusion—a quantity of arms and other articles were lying about in disorder. 1 Sir James Ingham:. Might the damage have !,•een caused by some explosive substance ?—Wltnees : I have no doubt of it.—Sir James Ingham : The details-will, no doubt, be furnished by somebody else: but I will ask, did you est any persons injured ?—Witness : I did. not, but I know that ' persons did sustain injaries.—Sir James Ingham: Did, you. 'leek at the prisoner's bands? Had they the appearance of -those of a dock labourer ?,—Witness: They were coarse,. like those of a man who worked. The prisoner was then remanded for a.vreek. • , • The statement that another arrest has been mar...l is denied by the police, who have definite information that the accused is a native of county Cork, and be has beer in' America from four to five years, and returned to England in. Use autumn.

FOREIGN OPINION.—.AMERICA AND THE OUT- RAGES. WAstritooroN, Mom)As..—The Senate to-day. discussed Mr. Bayard's resolution expressing indignation at the explosions, in London and detestation of such crimes. Mr. Riddleber- ger (Virginia) moved that Mr., Bayard's resolution ehould) be referred to the Foreign Committee. He said that the rHouse ought to have fuller information before it voted such, a resolution. He had no sympathy. with dynamiters, but Le declined to vote for the resolution, which. I, might be interpreted as an expression of spa.- ' pathy with Ireland's enemies. It was known, he added, that there was =absolute war between England and . Ireland, so far as it was possible for Irishmen without a country to make war. The motion was lest by 55 votes to two, Mr. Riddleberger and Mr. Van Wyck (Nebraska) being. the only senators who supported it. Mr. Bayard's resolu- tion was finally carried by 63 votes against one, the dissen- tient vote being that of Mr. Riddleterger.—ln the House of Representatives, Mr. Findlay (Maryland) proposed a resolu- tion calling upon the Secretary of State for information as to whether any citizen of the United States, or persons domiciled in the United States, were concerned, or had par- ticipated, directly or indirectly, in the explosions in Lon- don.

NEW Yorar, MONDAY.—A meeting of Socialists bas been held at Chicago, at which the recent outrages in London ' were applauded, and the free use of dynamite against capit- alists was advised. The New Y or& Herald, after denounc- ing these outrages and expressing the loathing felt by all Americans for the dynamite fiends, continues-4 It is no question of Irish independence ; on that theme we are never wearied of giving our views. It is a question of dastardly assassination. If moral law exics, if society is bound to- gether by any other code than that of accident, we de- clare that this leprosy must be stamped out now and for ever. _

A Paris correspondent says that these explosions are part y directed from the French capital. At all events some of the meat notorious Fenians are still lurking in the French capital, and they cross and recross horn France to England with impunity. In Vienna the outrage is generally put down to the An- archists, between whom and the Fenians no distinction is established abroad. Any attempt to explain the difference is met by the argument that in England all such crimes are attributed to the unlucky Irishman, but that dynamite is the monopoly of the Anarchists' and that England is paying the penalty of not joining the international league against them. The outrages in London are producing an im.nense sen- sation in Rome. The Rassegna says two conises suggest themselves—tirst, an insistence more energetic than hither- to that the United States shall use activity in prevent— ing the plotting of crime; secondly, the adhesion of England to the German and Russian League against anarchy, a course which no genuine Liberalism could die. approve. _ _ . .
Tho Madrid newspapers of all shades of opinion are unanimous in condemning as infamous the disgraceful at- tempt to destroy the Houses of Parliament.

At the Tower on Tuesday, a discovery was made which will, it is thought, have important bearings upon the man- ner in which the outrage was carried out. The soldiers in turning over the debris near the wall against which the ex. plosion occurred, found beneath a number of rifles which had been hurled to the ground by the concussion, the re- mains of an umbrella and remnants of a Woman's skirt. These articles may, of coarse, have belonged to one of the young women injured by the explosion, but the probabilities certainly do not point to such an explanation. As far as is known, none of the persons injured were at the moment of the explosion near the spot at which the dynamite was placed by the conspirators. Had they been within a yard or two they must have sustained the full force of the ex- plosive energy. But the wounds they received were Com- paratively trivial, and mostly caused by flying particles of metal. The balanoeof probability would, therefore, seem to be in favour Of the theory that the garment of which the remains only were found formed the outside wrapping of the infernal machine.

It has transpired that a letter was received at the General Post-office on Monday warning the authorities that a plot was in existence to blow up the Post-office buildings. It is believed that similar warnings have been received at other public departments, and although no exaggerated import- ance is attached to them, they have served to justify the special measures of precaution already taken. The char- acter of these precautions may be estimated by the fact that at Somerset House detectives have. been placed in all the departments accessible to the public, in addition to other safeguards which, for Obvious re.tsons, it is not advisable to particularise.

Mr. Qailliam, solicitor, Liverpool, has been instructed to defend the prisoner Cunningham, Linda arrest on susicion of being concerned in causing the explosion at the Tower; and the necessary fees have been lodged. Mr. Quilliam is the solicitor who defended Walsh, at Liverpool, about a year ago, when the latter was arrested in possession of dynamite bombs.

SATURDAY, JANUARY 31, 1885.

A THRILL of horror ran through the nation on Saturday evening when it became known that the Dynamite Conspirators had made an attempt to destroy the Houses of Parliament and the Tower of London ; and that, al- though they had not been wholly successful, they had done a great amount of damage and seriously injured a number of people. !The failure of the recent attempt to do seri- ous injury to London Bridge seems to have nerved the cowardly ruffians to strike at the seat of authority, and hence the three ex- plosions on Saturday afternoon—one at the Tower and two at Westminster. Cowardly the miscreants are, for there is not a spark of the heroic, however misguided, in laying an explosive parcel in a public building, and then sneaking off with the consciousness that, when it has done its worst, innocent men may be found to have been killed—men, for any- thing the wretches could know to the con- trary) in active sympathy with Ireland's cause. The selection of Saturday for these latest explosions is horrible in its atrocious- ness, for the conspirators could not but be aware that this was the day when in all pro- bability there would be large numbers of sight- seers both at the Tower and at the Houses of Parliament, For war against tyrants, or supposed tyrants, there may be some pallia- tive; but there is none for war against people who are as "Innocent as the child unborn." Murder most foul, as in the best it is,

But this is most foul, strange, and uunatural ; for if one or both of the policemen who were so seriously injured should die, there can be no question that the perpetrators of these wild outrages would be guilty of the gravest offence recognised by the law. The question is indeed raised whether, apart from any loss of life, the punishment of the offenders, if they are discovered, should not be one of death for the crime which they have com- mitted. Modern law, as administered in this country, recognises two offences only as meriting the capital sentence, and these are murder and high treason. There can be no doubt as to what constitutes murder; but what is high treason ? In plain terms it is levying war against the reigning sovereign; and, it he can be adjudged a traitor who levies war in ordinary form against the Queen, it seems to us that the Dynamiters ought not to escape the highest possible punishment because of the extraordinary way in which they are making war upon this country. The man who kills another under provocation, and in a moment of passion, is a saint com- pared with the monsters who would wan- tonly destroy people whom they have never ' even seen. There is hope of the offenders in this case being captured, and if they are it is some satisfaction to know that if they be not sentenced to death they will be liable 1

under the Explosive Substances Act to penal servitude for life. We do not know whether flogging would be a part of their punish- ment ;if not, it ought to be. The Garrotter is no worse than the Dynamiter. It is natural to ask—What can the Con," spirators hope to attain by their mad rooti.,ei of warfare? If it be supposed that it vir' in some way serve the cause of Ireland, thel It are cherishing a gross delusion. have the very reverse effect. Englishmen are menable to reason, but they will not yieldg fear. The danger rather is that the sul,° dering feeling of indignation at tne" atrocities which stirs every honest heart mai' if they are continued, be fanned into a flarnge which it would be difficult to subdue. would be a terrible day for Ireland and Irish" men if Englishmen, who are long.sufferi:l3os and slow to anger, should, letting Pa,ss.;°Of get the better of judgment, pursue a ponci - reprisal. It is not that men in auth°i rity, whether local or imperial, 14,,euni 0 ever think of such a thing; if uff-ill at all, it would be done by rash, vens men overriding the law and taking matter in their own hands. There was a suggesti° of what was possible in the rioting at Tortet' after the murder of Lord FREDERICK CAvs`; DISH, when the Irishmen of Turton wrer, driven out of the village, Happily, s°.'aci! there is no trace of a feeling of this 10n5,,, and, so long as no lives are lost, the Orli; munity, after the first shock, can witness 'lb spectacle of a destruction of property w, te something of calmness if not with abso'gb, equanimity. And need it be said that Ir,isto men as well as Englishmen will be taxe° make good whatever public property rilaY Qt destroyed. It is a poor way of serving Pat—thus to add to his heavy burden. mother of Mr. PARNELL has already deciarn-is that the explosions will injure her sei."4 work, and we can well believe her furri'''at statement that he was so discouragedmt the time of the Phcenix ?ark murders -0 he was at the point of giving up his effortS behalf of Ireland. This is language in„ttle right vein; it is the right view to take or; if situation; and we should have been gla:hto Mr. PARNELL himself had—as he oug,11:„6 have done—sized the opportunity in 1,10 on Monday of denouncing the dastards are putting obstacles in his path. It is t"ci duty of Irishmen to speak out quicklY strongly; and thus show themselves 151 matter in harmony with the common Old, ment of the New as well as of the Old W°,,raa It is gratifying to observe that our Arneoo cousins, hitherto slow to move, are 12 is taking speedy action. Rapid progress to being made with a bill which seeks to enact that it shall be felonious to manufacteeg, or export dynamite for criminal purP°stbe This may not go far enough to get at. 0, real evil ; but it is in the right directiflc What is more, it is backed by a Pul'iy opinion which is for the first time strongat asserting itself; and it may thus happen twit it will be followed, if required, by a ;te which will put those in prison who advo''f'„g murder in England as a means of impr°v,l;s ; the condition of Ireland. The CYDON°Y4 ROSSAS have long cried—" Down with eveils; thing English " ; it is now time to ra'r,t the cry—" Down with the O'DoNoll ROSSAS

the hands of the enemy; and there is a burning desire on the part of some of our officers to drive them out. But to what end? Our troops are now in communication with Rhartoum, and General GORDON • and his followers can, if required, be brought away Without touching Metemmeh. It should be kept in mind that the object of the expedition IS not the destruction of the Soudanese, but t, he rescue of General GORDON. Of course, the enemy continue to give our • soldiers trouble' the rebels, as they ar,s called, will be troubled in return; it is to be hoped they are be- ginning to realise that they had better keep Out of the way. Lord WOLSELRY has laid his plans most skilfully; for while one body of _

Theo is on its way to reinforce the troops ibat have crossed the desert, a river force, under the command of General EARLE, is going up the Nile to Berber. This latter numbers 2,400 men, and has already given a good ac- count of itself in a skirmish with the troops Of the MARDI. As will be seen from the Thap which we give to-day of the seat of war, Lord WOLSELEY Wilt shortly be in a position to cover the whole of the horse-shoe bend of ,the Nile, unless,the enemy are in a position ° Make i stoat resistance at Berber. BLEEPING Our.-On Tuesday, Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, Jan., sitting at Widnes Police Carat, sentenced John hilihee, of Liverpool, and Thomas Walker, a native of Southport, described as tramps, to seven days' bard labour each for sleeping in the salt cake shed at the Widnes Alkali COmpany's works on the previous night. Mutat os limecosts ScstoONEs —At five o'clock on Thursday morning, the schooner Princess Marie, of Run- corn (Isaac Folks master), from Waterford to Port William, was driven ashore on the rocks near Maughold Head, Isle Of Man, and became a total wreck. The crew of three men took to their boat, and, having rounded the head and got under shelter of the land, pulled to Ramsey. 'I he vessel, which had a cargo of bones, has since disappeared. A WESTON GROCER FINED.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, before Mr. W. Banks and Mr. C. Reynolds, Edward Jones, grocer, Weston, was charged with having in his possession for the use of trade a pair of scales which were unjust. On the 20th instant Superintendent Leah Visited the defendant's shop, and found a pair et scales 5 drachms out of balance against the purchaser. A brass ball, which ought to be secured permanently to the scales, was loose. A fine of 10s. and costs was imposed. Tam or IRON AT WIDNIES.—Before Mews. F. H. Go. sage and J. Brock, at Widnes Police Court. on Monday, Margaret Wall, of Elizabeth-street, Newtown, was charged with stealing 121tIbs, of iron belonging to Messrs. James Muepratt and Sons. On Saturday morning P.S. Strickland met the prisoner in Ann-street West, and observed that she was attempting to conceal a large piece of iron beneath her shawl. When she saw the officer she dropped the iron. It was afterwards discovered that it belonged to Messrs. Mnspratt. The prisoner was sentensed to 2/. days hard labour.

It appeared that for several years the prisoner had lived at Frodsharn, but recently he had taken UP his abode at Patricroft, near Man- chester. STONE BREARELS ON STRIKE AT WIDNES.—About two , months ago, when the weather was cold and winterly, there I was considerable talk about the large number of men in the town who were unable to obtain work, aud the destitu- tion into wblchstany families were plunged inconsequence. The Local Board, in order to alleviate this distrees, deter- mined to associate philanthropy with their usual hard matter-of-fact duties, and engaged about 80 of the unem- ployed men to work for the ratepayers. About forty of these were deputed to help in repairing and cleaning the roads of the town, and the rest were tat to stone breaking. Tue latter were paid at the rate of 2s per cubic yard, with a person to ' sledge" for them, but it was decided subse- quently to pay them at the same cats as the permanent stone breakers for the Board, viz., 2s 3d per cubic yard, each man to sledge for himself. The whole e the costs would have to be borne by 'Use defendant. FATHER NuGENr AT WIDNES. Under the auspicet of the Widnes Branch of the League ,of the Cross, the Ray. Father Nugent, of Liverpool, on Tuesday evening delivered a lecture in the Widnes Volun- ecer Hall in aid of the fund for extinguishing the debt upon Ct. Mary's Catholic Church. The buildieg was crowded with an audience composed of men and women of all sects and creeds, not lees than 1,200 persons being present, and the rev, father, whose philanthropic Monte in the seaport city are well known, received a flattering oration. Mr. T. Sutton Ticemis. J.P,, presided, and on theplatform or in elope proximity were the Revs. Fathers Clarke, Finegan, V. Feins, S.J. (Ditton College), Bruder, S.J. (Ditten College), Ryan. Oldham and Scannell (Warrington) ; O'Keeffe, Dr. McDonnell, MeCambridge, Messrs J. Morrison, A. Cow- ley, IL Matthews, W. Treacy, and D. Forster. Previous to the meeting St. Mary's Brass :Band and a good number of the members of the League of the Cross had promenaded the streets of the town, and during the proceedings they occu- pied a prominent position. The band played several selec- tions of music. The Chairman, who was cordially received, explained that when their friend Father Ryan asked him to take the chair that evening, he told him he wou,ld be very glad to do anything in hes power to oblige his friends and neighbours at Widaes--(applanse)—but that there was this difficulty ; that meeting was held under the sleepless of the League of the Cross, and he (the Chairman) was not a teetotaler. (tepplause and laughter.) Father Ryan said he supposed he was an advocate ef temperance, and on his replying in the affirmative he said he could very well occupy the position that evening. (Applause.) Although he was not a teetotaller he yielded to no man in that as- sembly in his admiration of temperance principles. (Ap- plause) He believed that the spread of temperance Peinciplem was doing an inealculable amount of good in the country, Although trade wee admittedly bad everywhere,

yet it was most astonishing to find from the statistics published recently that the sums deposited ie the savings bank had increased ; the number of paupers, of criminals, and of lunatics had decreased, and all these good reeults, he believed, were mainly owing to the spread of temperance principles. He was therefore a hearty supporter of V) e Cause whose interests they were met that evening to ad- vocate. (Applause.) He then introduced the Rev. Father Nugent, who was greeted with enthusiastic applause. The rev. gentleman, after a few introductory remarks, delivered his popular' lecture on "The power of the penny," which had special referenoe to the temperance cpsestron. His observations, which were freveatly ap- plauded, were illustrated by capital views thrown upon a screen by the oxy-hydrogen lantern. Afterwards Mr. McCarthy, of the League Hall, Liverpool, sang several temperance melodies, and gave recitations in his usual dramatic style. On the proposition of Dr. O'Kettfe. seconded by the Rev. Father Rya, a hearty vote of thaake was accorded to the lecturer. In. replying, the Rev. Fetker Nugent alluded to the importance of providieg the people with genuine means of recreation after the laborious duties of the day. This had too lung been forgotten, and ' what priest or clergyman of any deneminatian would not rejoice and be glad on Sunday if he had such a fine body of ,nen and women to address himself to as he saw before him to address himself to. (applause.) Speaking of the practical side of the temperance question, the rev, father said his twenty-one years' experience at the gaol at Walton had convinced him of the absolute necessity of their people abstaining from in- toxicating drink. Out of the 170,000 prisoners who had passed under his charge, he was prepared to assert that not one who had suffered the slightest material injury by breaking the bottle and cutting the tap all at once. (Ap- plause.) At the close of this address a large number of per- sons took the pledge in a aulemn manner, and the meet- ing terminated.
WIDNES TRADERS' ASSOCIATION. ANNEAL MEETING.

A meeting of the members of this Assoeatison was held on Tuesday afternoon in the officers' room of the Drill Hall. Mr. E. K. Muspratt presided, and there were present Cept. Brunner, Messrs. T. S. Timmis, W. Vickers, Liddell, and H. W. Deacon (hon. secretary). The Hon. Secret try read the annual report as follows : "At the last general meeting the committee was authorised, in order to opppose the London ant North-Western Railway Bill, to make a levy of not exceeding 3d in the pound on the gross annual value of the members' work., and a levy of 21e1 was made. Other traders in Widnes not being mem- bers of the Association were requested to subscribe their share. Three firms responded to the invitation, and a depa- ,l rate account was opened at the bank. The statement show- ing the amount of subscriptions and the expeaditure from the special fund will b 3 found in the statement of accounts, No. 2, given below. It will be remembered that the London and North- Western Railway Company proposed in their bill of last session to take powers to provide wagons for the coal traffic and to make charges to which the Association obj,cted. The Executive Committee in carrying into effect the resolution, passed at the last general meeting, lodged a petition in the House of Commons against the bill. The railway company Opposed the locus slassdi of the traders, and the case was argued before the referees, who decided in favour of the traders. Some members of the Executive Committee went to London and had an interview with the reptesentatives of the railway company. Nothing, however, was arraoged at the interview, though ultimately the railway company withdrew the clause, and the matter ended. • Last session a bill "to amend the Regulation of Railways Act and for other purposes" was introduced into the House of Commons by Mr. Chamberlain. There were some points In the bill, especially the clause in which it was proposed to give the railway companies power te make terminal charges to which traders gerierelly throughoet the kingdom ob- jected. The Executive Committee sent the hon. sec. te terra one of a deputation organised by 'the Railway and Can:.•l Traders' Association to wait on Mr. Chamberlaie and ex- I press the views of traders and urge amendments in the bill. The deputation was raVOtr received by Mr. chamber- lain; but Il the end the bill was not proceeded with on account of pressure of public business in Parliament. The Railway and Canal Traders' Association, to which reference has already been made, has been for some time issaing a journal, and the committee arranged to take a suf- ficient number of copies to allow of one being sent to each member of the Association. The journal contains same Me, ful information, and, if properly supported, ought to become a valuable paper. The pro noters of the Manchester Ship Canal have again introduced a bill, and they now propose to construct the canal on the Cleashire side of the river. It is feared that the works, if constructed, may as alter the channels in the river that the ioterests of all Widnes traders will be most ' seriously affected, and there are not in the bill any clauses which sufficiently protect those interests. The Widnes Loci! Board is giving its attention to the bill, and will op- pose, if necessary; but velar committee recommends that your Association should also oppos-, unless negotiations now in progress should end successfully, as it is of vital import- lance that the trade of Widnes should not be injured by the 1 const: action of the Ship ."..)anal. The London and North-WeAern Railway Company is in- troducing two bide, by one of which it is proposed to make a new dock at Garston alid to authoez a certain alterations in the charges which now apply lo the old dock. Your committee contends that the new dock should for the pur- poses of rates and charges be ineluded in the expression, ..Garstnu Dock," in the Transfer Aot, and that no altera- tions in the charges authorized by that Act should be sanctioned. Negotiations have la:en entered into with the solicitore for the railway company, but your committee recommends that, if a satisfactory result be not obtained, the Association oppose the hill. Several of the large railway compenies, the Loecion and No: th-Western Midi end, aud Great Northern, amongst them, have introduced Bills in which they declare the rates and I charge to be made in resvct of the conveyance of traffic ion their respect.ve lines of railway. All the Bills are based I on the same general principles and adopt the clearing house classification as the basis for their proposed classification, while it is proposed that, in addition to the mileage rate, the railway c :nap aniessh all have power to make it " reason- . able charge" for terminals.

• Your committee does net otij-ct to the railway companies having power to charge for terminal eervices which are de- fined and rendered, provided that the mileage rates are fair and reasonable, but when the mileage rates alone, for dis- tances under twenty miles, are in almost ail instances to be higher than the maximum rates of the old Acts, it is impos- sible to accept the present Bills as the result of a reasonable attempt on the part of the railway companies to settle the vexed question of terminal charges. Your committee will memorialize the Board of Trade and do all it can by drawing the attention of the county and other members of Parliament to the Bills to secure their rejec- tion on their second reading, but if they pass the second read- ing your committee recommends that the Associationoffer the most strenuous opposition, unless the Bills are modified to meet the traders' views. .

-- lf it prove necessary to carry out the opposition to the bills referred to, a considerable sum. of money will be required, and the funds in band are not sufficient. As will be seen from the statement, No. 1, given below, the balance on December rd to the credit of toe tBB7 account, which is the general account of the association, was £9l 7s 9d. The then outstanding accounts aril-elated to £64 15s 3i, and, as they have since been paid, there is now only a balance of £26 12513.1 to the credittf that fund. Lest year ' a separate account was opened for the purpose of opposing the Linden and North-Western Railway Bill, and the 'balance after prying the expensevof the opposition is fs7s 93 fid, as shown in statement N0..2. The three firms, not members of the association, subscribed their share of the levy for the special purpose on the understanding that their share of any helance their might be should be returned ea them. Their shares amount to £43 15s Bd, and it will thus be seen that there will remain a balance of £331 13s 101 Your committee recommends that the London and North- Western opposition accouet, 2.584, be closed, and that the balance, and with their consent, the shares of the noz-mem- bare be transferred to a fresh account to be called the 4. Widnes Traders' Canal and R ailway Opposition Account, 1885 e" a n d it further recommends that it he authorised to snake afresh levy, if necessary, of not exceediug 3d in the £ on the gross annual value of each membet's works." : The Chairman moved the adoption of the report, and re- ferred to the various matters which had engaged the atten- tion of the committee during the past year. Alluding to railway rates and charges, the Chairman said in order to settle the.tquestion in an equitable manner, it was clearly neceesary that the whole question of rates and charges should be referred not to a ceaamittee of the loam of Commons, which was incapable of dealing with a complicated technical matter of that kind, but to a body like the Railway Corn- miseioners who were experts, who had had for several years the.question of arta.xitnum rates brought before them, and who would be fully qualified to deal with a question of that kind and see that the interests of the public were safe- guarded. The point of appeal was also a very important one becauee .one of the great advantages of the Railway Commissioners Court at the present time was that there was no appeal from its decisioas on questions of fact. The ques- tion of these rates and charges came up again this session in rather another shape. The Railway Companies had lodged bills with a view to a new classification of goods based on the clearing house qualification, but when they came to ex- amine these bills they found that for all short distances, if they were adopted, the haders would really be in a worse state than they were under the present law. He thought it was to the interest of the Association to oppose the bills to the greatest extent in their power. In this opposition the Association would be joined by the tea. ions trading and agricultural associations throughout the country, who were now beginning to find what they in Widnes had discovered long ago that railway companies wherever they had prac- tically a monopoly in any trade, as they had in chernictls, they would charge the highest rate they possibly could if to their opinion it wculd not endanger the traffic. Speaking of the Ship Canal Bill, the Chairman said engineers who were conversant with the river, were of opinion that if the canal was carried out as proposed, would cause the silting up of the entrances to the Widnes Docks. This prac- tically would be the destruction of the trade of Widnes. At any rate it would throw the whole trade of Widnes to Gaston, or some place having shipment of goods through the canal. This matter was of such immense importance that he was sure the association would be only too glad to combine with the Local Beard who represented the whole town in opposing this scheme mules they coeld get such a

clause inserted io the Hill that would safeguard the interests of the community, Mr T 8 Timmis seconded the motion. He said that al- though the London an North-Western Rtilway Cornpany withdrew their bill last year, the traders were put to con- siderable expense, b3canse they had to employ a solicitor in Liverpool, and they had also to appear before the referees be' counsel. Those traders' who, whilst not members of the association, had subscribed to its funds, might think this explanation needed. He thought in the future the railway company would be satisfied to meet their wishes without this unnecessary expense. Speaking of the work of the association for the next year, Mr Timmis said since the for- mation of the association there had been no subjects of equal importance. Their moat vital interests were attacked, and ' it behove I the association to opppose the bills most Strenu- ously. 1 _. . . .

The report was adopted unanimously. Resolutions were passed authorising the Executive Com- mittee to oppose the Manchester Ship Canal, certain eauses in the London and North Western Bill relating to the charges at Garston Dock, the bills of the London and North Western. the Midland, and the Great Northern Rail- ways, declaring the rates and charges to be made for the conveyance of traffic, and that the president on behalf of the association sign petitions against the bills. The Exe- cutive Committee was also authorised for the purpose of carrying into effect the foregoing resolutions to transfer the balance of the London and North Western, opposition account, 1884, to a new acccnnt to be called "The Widnes Traders' Railway and Canal Opposition Account for 1885," and to make a levy of not exc=eding 31. in the £ on the groes anneal value of each member's works as it now stood in the poor-rate books of the township. On the motion of Mr. Brunner, seconded by Mr. Vickers, it was resolved that the non-rremb.-rs who subrcribed to the Loudon and North Western opposition account of last year be requested to , allow the hrlance to be transferred to the new account, and I also again to subscribe their there of the freso levy, on the understanding that their share of any balance that may be left should be returned to them. A vote of thanks was accorded to the Chairman and Executive Committee for the way in which they had watched the interests of the Widnes Trad• re' Association lurine. the past year and pre- vious years, on the motion of Mr. Vickers, seconded by Mr. Liddell.

The anniversary of the Lymm branch of the Warrington district of the order of Shepherds, was held at the Nag s Head Hotel, on Tuesday, when an excellent dinner was provided by the Misses Win- stanley, of the above Hotel. After the cloth was removed Mr R Ditchfield war voted to thc chair, supported by the Past Worthy Chief of the lodge. The secretary, Mr George Li Leigh, gave a very eatisfactery report on the progress of the Lymm branch. The bankiag account was over doubled in Eve years. Looking at every point, he could say the lodge was in a dourishing pcsition. lie would like it to be known that a juvenile secietir had been formed and was working well. The trea.sucer, Mr Ditchfield, spoke of the pleasure it gave him to be with them, and of the satisfactory way the business of the lodge was done. Thanks were given to the chairman for presiding, and to those who con- ducted the musical programme, also to the Misses Winstan- ley for their excellent catering.

A Fox IN k CITEMCAL Worms. A singulat incident occurred at St Helens on Thursday, when a young fox was discovered on the premises of Messrs Kurtz, chemical man- ufacturers, Warrington-road. Some commotion was caused among the men, who attempted to secure it, but the animal ran about the work O and various furnaces, and at last took refuge beneath one of the chemical chambers where it re- mained for several hours. The noxious fumes from the chemicals evidently had an eff!ct upon" Master Reynard," who expired in his hiding place. It was at first supposed that the animal was a fox which had been driven into the town from Garswood Park, the estate of Lord Gerard, but it was eventually elaimed by Mr. Rudge, of tha St. Helens Gasworks, who lives in Sutton-road, Peasley Cross. The animal was about twelve months old, and was brought from South Wales nine months since. During the day it was allowed to roam In the yard and go into a" run" which had been specially constructed for it, and at night it was fastened up in a box. After being fed on Thursday morning it escaped and wandered over the waste ground, through the premises of Messrs Reurnes and Robinson,colliery pro- prietors, and thence into the works of Messrs Kurtz, were its death occurred as stated above.

Rzcarknore or LORD RIPON.—A public reception was accorded to the Marquis of Ripon on Tuesday by the citizens of Ripon, the local gentry, and the tenants on his lordship's estate, on the occasion of the return of the noble Marquis after an absence of five years in India. On his journey from York his lordship was presented at Harrogate with an address of welcome from the young Corporation of that place. Upon the arrival of the Marquis at Ripon he was met at the station by the Bishop of the diocese, the Dean, Mr. Goshen, M.P., the local magistrates, the tenantry, and the friendly societies, who, headed by the Hussars and local volunteers, formed a procession from the railway station to the city, a distance of nearly a mile. Ad- dresses were presented by the Mayer and Corporation and the Mechanics' Institution. On Wednesday night the Mar- quis of Ripon was entertained at a " welcome home " ban- quet in the Leeds Town Hall. Sit Edward Baines presided, and there was a brilliant assemblage, including Mr. Childers and Mr. Forster. On Thursday the Marquis of Ripon received at Ripon a further series of demonstra- tions of welcome on the occasion of his return from India. In the forenoon he ,visited the Yorkshire Co:lege at Leeds, and subsequently he received in Ripon Town Hall an ad- dress from the tenantry of hl3 Yorkshire estates, to whom he promised early and careful consideration of the state of agriculture in the district. Later in the afternoon his lord- ship received an address from the teachers and scholars of St. Wilfrid's Roman Catholic School. In the evening he briefly spoke at a tea given to about 1,200 of the working classes in the large wooden pavilion.

----- WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATIIRDIY.—Before Aldermen Chandley and Burgess. DRUNIEENNESS.—MArgaret Baguley, last from Liverpool, hawker, was fined 5s and costs, or seven days' imprison- ment, for being drunk and disorderly in Horsemarket•street on the previous day. Motrnait.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) in the . _

chair, and Mi. John Fairclough. MISCELLANEOUS—The following cases of drunkenness were dealt with :—James Peers, at Townsend, on Saturday evening, fined 5s including costs ; Ann Griffin, in Bridge-, street, on Saturday evening, fined 53 including costs ; Catherine Hankinson, on Cropper's-brow, on the 9th inst. fined 53 and costs.--Bridget Walsh, charged with keeping edgers without having her house registered, was dismissed with a caution ;William Yates was lined 10a and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment, on a similar charge.---Mary Ellen Marsh was charged with hawking without a license, and was dismissed on promising to procure one.--George Higharn, for allowing a band-cut to remain in Bridge-street an unreasonable length of time, was tined 5s including costs.--Arthur Gill, for wheeling a truck on a footpath on the 20th inst, was fined Is Oct including costs.--Elizibeth Boston was fined 2s 6d. including costs, for a similar offence.—James Kenyon was tined is Oct and costs for allowing his chimney to be on fire on the 17th inst. A LAZY VAGRANT.—Thomas Miskell, a young man, was Sent to gaol for 14 days fer breaking out of the vagrant ward at the Warrington Union without having performed his task Of Work. Frltiors Dramo.-11snry Wardle was summoned for furiously driving a horse and trap in Bridge-street on the 19th inst. He was fined 103 and costs. TEESDAY.—Before Councillor C. Broadbent. BEGGlNG.—Elizabeth Ball, elderly woman, native of Shrop- shire, was charged with begging in Buttermarket-street on the previous afternoon. She was dismissed on promising to leave the town.

FRlDAY—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) and Alderman Holmes. REFUSING TO WORK —John Noon was charged with re- fusing to perform his task of work whilst an inmate of the vagrant ward of thc Union. It was 11,1 s 64th appearance.— Committed for seven days. DRUNKENNES9.—Ann Griffin was sent to prison for seven days for being drunk and disorderly in Iklman's-line the previous evening. A Carr-rots vo Boys.—George Sankey, Thomas Travis, Edward Clare, and Thomas Edwards were each flied is, including costs, and severely censured for playing at "shinty "in the public streets. John Carroll was fined 2s 6d and costs for playing at "peggy." MASTER AND APPRENTICE.—Winifred Kilcourse sum- moned William Hockenhall, master fus'ian cutter, for a breach of apprenticeship indentures, by causing her to lose' time through loss of work. There was a counter chim of 12s for neglect of work by the girl. The Bench awarded Klcourse tia and dismissed the counter chin.

DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS. TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. Marson, W. Long, and R. Pierpoint. DRUNKENNESS —Samuel Massey, Frank Beach, and John Britton were charged with having been drunk and disorderly at Little Leigh on the 27th ult., and were each fined 5s and costs.—Joho Miller, for a similar offence at Stretton OR the 3rd January, was fined 5s and costs. A NEGLIGENT DRIVER.—Samuel Smith, a young man, was charged with having been negligent whilst in charge of a horse and cart.—s—lt was stated that on the night of the 9th 'lost the defendant's horse and cart were left at the door of a public•houss at Stretton without anyone in charge, and afterwards ran away down the road to War• rington.—The defendant said he was a driver in the employ of Mr. Fairhurst, gingerbeer maker, Warrington, and was In the public-house soliciting orders In the usual way.—A fine Of 53 and costs was imposed. AN ABSCONDING FEMALE —Sarah ffarris Clarke, who was charged with stealing X-I belonging: to her brother-in-law, a man named Brocklehurst, living at Antrobus, did not put in an appearance. She had prsviouslv been before the Oc- csional Court at Warrington, and was -by that court allowed out on her own recognisances. It was now, however, stated by the police that she had disappeared, and her whereabouts was not known.— A warrant was granted.
PRESCOT PETTY SESSIONS. TuESDAY.—Before Mr. F. W. Fate.

MitcELLlNEonS.—P—airiCir Hannasey (Huyton) was bound 'over to keep the macs for two months for committing a 'breach of the peace at Huyton, on the 231 h nit.—Michael Dolan, for being drunk and disorderly at Huyton, on the 23th nit., was fined 5s and costs.—Paul Molyneux was fined 7s t3d and costs for being drunk and disorderly at Frescot, and a like penalty v: as imposed on John Lyon for a like offence committed at Huyton Quarry.—Alexander Glover (Huyton) and John Ellis (Whiston) were also fined 7s 6d and costs for drunkennese.—James Cave for commit- ting a breach of the psace at Huyton, on the 3rd inst., was bound over to keep the peace for two months.—For being drunk and incapable in Tarbock, John Chorley was fined 5s and costs.—A like penalty was imposed on John White- house, for a similar offence at Huyton. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE.—James Brittleton, labourer, Tar- "bock, was summoned for ne ' glectino• to send his child to school, and the Bench made an order for the law to be com- plied with. _ .
GAMING AT WHISTON.—Edward Spark, William Chest- barn, Joseph Jones, and Richard Evans, all of Whiston, were summoned for playing at pitch and toss at Whiston, and were fined 5s and costs each.

DRIVERS IN TROUBLR.—Henry Smith, for leaving his cart on the highv.ay at Roby longer than necessary on the 10th inst. was fined 28 61 and costs.—Henry Holden. for riding on the shaft of his cart without reins, in Warrington. road, Whiston, on the 10th inst., was fined 2s 61 and costs. —Henry Hogan, Rabohill, for riding without reins at Rain- hill, on the 10th inst., was fined 2s fid and costs.—John Riding was fined 2s 61 and costs for being asleep in his cart at Raiahill, on the 17th inst.

THE SOUDAN CAMPAIGN,
TELEGRAMS PROM LORD WOLISELEY
MARCH OF GENERAL EARLE ON BERBER. Telegram from General Lord Weiseley to the Secretary *of State for War :

"Kurd, Jan. 24, 140 p.m.—General Earle's column, to- gether with soma guns and cavalry and camel troops, star- ted this morning from flandab for Berber, via Abu Ahmed. The enemy, consisting of the Monassir tribe, under Wad Garnr, the murderer of Col. Stewart, and others under Moussa, have collected at Birti, 25 miles above Handab. They say they mean fighting, but as reports received say General Stewart's victory has created a great effect everywhere, it is d tubtful if Earle will meet with serious opposition until he reaches Berber. The health of the troops is excellent. They are in the highest sprite, and proud of the recent success. It is very doubtful if the reported capture of Omdurman by the enemy be true. No further news re- ceived yet from Stewart of condition of wounded at Abu Klea." •

Lord Wolseley telegraphed to the War Office from Kora on Monday morning that there was no cause for anxiety owing to the absence of news of Sir Herbert Stewart's force. The news of the 17th, he says, was brought by Bashi- Bazouks, of whom there are no more with Stewart'a force, and further intelligence must, therefore, come by camel with an ordinary British escort. Immediately this telegram was received it was sent to the Queen. HANDAB, SINDAY.—Tbe main body of General Earle's column started yesterday. Three boats with skilled officers and Canadian crews nnder Colonel Alleyne, left shortly after daybreak, going ahead as scouts to the column. They were followed by two companies of the South Staffordshire Regiment acting as the advanced guard. A boat load of men of the 26th Company of Royal Engineers, under Cap- tain Blackburn, led the main column of whalers. Simulta- neously Colonel Butler advanced on the river bank with forty Husears and the Egyptian cavalry. They will care- fully reconoitre the country as they proceed, and render any sudden attack upon the boats impossible. General Earle, with his staff, followed later ou, and a party of Hussars started along the bank, acting as a rear-guard to the colnmn. The whole body halted for the night at Owli Island. The boats arrived in the course of the afternoon, having experienced no great difficulty in the passage. MaNnen, MONDAY.—Generai Earl's column advanced six miles yesterday, and ascended the series of rapids above Owli Island. Upon the whole the stream is not so swift and powerful as had seen expected from the native reports, but there were many stretches of broken water, when it needed all the efforts of the troops to get the boats up. No signs of the Arabs were to be seen. Colonels Butler and Alleyne reconnoitred the country still further in advance towards the ener.ny'e position, but with a like result. Colonel Col. yule, with the aladir's Soudanese troops, is en the right bank of the river abreast of the boats. He keeps in com- munication with them by heliograph.--Standard. The following official telegram is from the War Office: "From Lord Woleeley, Korti, Jan. 27, 9-25 a.m.—Re- port, dated yesterday, just in from General Earle. His force is making most satisfactory progress up the river. I sent a large convoy yesterday to Gakdul, and expect to hear from General Stewart this evening or to-morrow." CAIRO, TUESDAL—Lieut-General Sir F. Stephenson has received a telegram from Lord Wolseley announcing that General Earle's column is now beyond the Fourth Cataract, and is moving on quite right. Lord Wolseley expects to receive news from General Stewart to-day or to-morrow, and adds that there is no reason for anxiety.
GREAT BATTLE NEAR DIETEMBIEH. ANOTHER BRITISH VICTORY. GENERAL STE ViTART WOUNDED. GORDON RELIEVED. LORD WOLSE LEY'S DESPATCH.

Lord Hartington received the fcllowing important despatch from General Lord Wolseley early on Wed- nesday morning:— From General Lord Wolseley to Seeretary of State for War, received January 28th, 6-40 a.m. (telegram No. 29) : Kora; WEDNESDAY' 5 a.m. Captain Pigott, Mounted Infantry, just arrived from Gabat, on the Nile, two miles above Hetemmeh, which he left on the 24th inst.

There has been some sharp fighting since the action on the 17th inst., and the men have had. ex- tremely hard work, and until the 23rd inst., little sleep. General Stewart, who I deeply regret has been severely wounded, has carried out my instructions, and we have now a strongly fortified position on the Nile, half way between Berber and Khartoum,aud we hold the desert route between it and this place. On the large island opposite Gaba.t there is plenty of green forage for horses and camels. Gnbat can be held against any force the lltrandi can send to attack it.

Four steamers from Khartoum, under Nusri Pasha, arrived at Gubat during the reconnaissance made on Metemrneh on the 2lst'inst. The Pasha landed men and guns and took part in the operations. Sir C. iiirdson left for Khartoum on the 24th inst., with two steamers and a detachment of the Sussex Regiment. Metemmeh is occupied by about 2,000 of the enemy, half of whom are regulars under Nu r Angar, who has three Krupp guns but very little ammunition for them. None of the hells fired from them exploded. At Shendy there is one Krupp gun and a small gar- rison.

A hospital has been established at Meternmeh, where the wounded are well eared for. The movements of General Stewart's forces since my last telegram were as follows : Having established a strong poet at Ahn Rica Wells, he left there about four p.m. on the r3th inst. After passing the wells at Shabacat, he moved to their right, as my instructions were that if Metein meh were held General Stewart should establish him- self on the Nile between it and Khart,,utn. About seven a.m. on the 19th instant, when three or four miles from the river, the enemy showed in force. A halt was made for breakfast in a strong zereba. It was here that General Stewart was wounded,

pulsed, however, with heavy loss, General Stewart placing it at 250 killed, with a large number wounded, while another account gives it as I,3oo,lrilled and wounded. Five of the Mandi's Emirs were killed, and the reverse was so thorongh as to utterly discourage the enemy from again assuming the offensive. Their bearing in this fight is de- clared by Sir Herbert Stewart not to be compared with the courage that was shown is the engagement at Abu Klea.

BRITISH LOSSES. The British loss was serious, but not nearly so severe as in the former engagement. Altogether' we lost 20 killed and 60 wounded, the killed including Quartermaster A G Lima, of the 19th Hussars, and Conductor of Supplies A C Jewel, of ttie Commissariat and Transport Corps. Two of the newspaper correspondents, who have distin- guished themselves in this and previous campaigns, were also killed—namely, Mr Cameron, of the Standard, and Mr St. Leger Herbert. of the Morning Post. The intelligence of the deaths of these two gentannen was transmitted to the proprietors of their respective j)urnals by Lord Wolso- ley's private secretary. The officers wounded were as follows: .
