div.head: ON TfiE
div.p: ON TfiE

On the 21st a reconnaissance in force was made of Met m- n3eh, which had been placed in a state of defence, and the walls loopholed. Daring this reconnaissance four steamers arrived from Khartoum at Gubat, on the banks of the Nile, two miles above Metemmeh. Nusri Pasha had command 61 the vessels, and he landed some men and guns and took part in the reconnaissance. A second reconnaissance was made on the 22nd on board Nusri Pashi's steamers, down the river as far as Shendy, where there was a small garrison of rebels, with one Krupp gun. The steamer returned, however, without havirg at- tacked the enemy, on the same day. Metemmeh is occupied by about 23G0 men of the Mandi's followers, half of whom are regulars, under Nur angari, who has three Knipp guns, but very little ammunition for them: The British troops were fired on from Metemmeh, but none of the shells from the guns exploded, they evi- dently being old and obsalete stores. Sir C. Wilson then advanced to Crubat, and there con- structed a post which be strongly fortified, and the troops were the on the 23rd able to gain a night's rest for the first time since the battle of Abu Klea. A hospital was estab- lished a little nearer Metemmeh, where the wounded were well carcd for, On 11P large Wand opposite Gabat there is plenty of green forage for norses and camels; and the place I can be held against any force the Mandi can send to attack it.

After seeing the expeditionary force safuly entrenched at Gubat, Sir Charles Wilson, taking a portion of the Sussex with him, started en the 24th inst. on hoard of one of Gor- don'e steamers, and taking a second steamer with him, for Khartoum. News from the gallant defender of that citadel may, therefore, be expected at an e lay date. MORE FIGHTING IN THE SOUDAN. GENERAL EA.RLE'S COLUMN ENGAGED. The Daily Telegraph's second edition of Thursday con- !s tabs the following telegram :—" Hamdab, Wednesday, 8 5 p.m.—On Tuesday the Black Watch and the htaffordshire Regiment arrived at the Fort of the Kabd-El-Abt cataract. The cavalry scouts changed shots with the enemy two miles in advance. The Arabs then attacked, but were driven back by the civalry and the camel corps, who occupied the vil- lage of Warag, previously held by the Mandi's forces. A number of cattle and sheep were captured. The enemy re- treated towards Birti. At daylight the column was to move forward agaih. The health of the trooops is most satisfactory. CONDITION OF THE WOUNDED. DESPATCH FROM LORD WOLSELEY.

Rolm, JANUARY 29re, 10-30 A m.-.-Natei from surgeon received from Uubat report th4t General, Stewatt is pro- gressing Moat favourably. He Is wonderfully free front in. flanunetory symptoms, and suffering comparatively little pain. No attempt, of course, to extract the bullet, which entered high up in groin. No bad symptoms. Every hope of rapid recovery. Hospi- tal pitched on bank of river. All housed under tents and on native beds. Considering the many moves and hard- ships, wounded doing wonderfully well. Two-thirds of cases severe. Number of operations will be large. Surgeon Magill distinguished himself before being wounded by shot in thigh All wounded, or as many as possible, to be sent back to Gakdul. Any amount of supplies if natives will bring them in. No sickness yet amongst troops. ANOTHER MESSAUE FROM THE QUEEN.

- The Queen receiv ,d, on Wednesday, the intelligence of the further success of Sir Herbert Stewart's column and of the engagement on the 19ch inst. and following days. While rejoicing at the victory gained by her gallant troops, Her Majesty has learnt with sincere regret the losses sustained, and laments deeply the wound to Sir Herbert Stewart, which has deprived her Majesty of a most valuable officer.

THE WARRINGTO INFIRMARY. MEETING OF THE WORKING-MEN'S REPRESENTATIVES. On Saturday afternoon a rnee.ing gf the representatives appointed by the enneloyes of various firms in the town to represent them on the Hoepital Working-men's Committee was held in the Mayor's Parlour, Town Hall. The Mayor presided, and in addition to a large attendance of represen- tatives there were present Alderman Davies, and Mr. Ziba Armitage, hon. secretary.—The minut•s of the previous meeting having been confirmed, Mr. ARMITAGE read a list of the contributione by the employes of the various contribu- ting firms, and also the other items of income in connection I with the Working-men's Committee, a statement of which we have previously given. There was, Mr. Armitage said, about £24 14s 23 less collected last year than in the pre- vious year. This -wail awing to several firms not having con- tributed, but who contributed the year previowsly. Had these firms continued to contribute in the same ratio as in the previous year there would have been a larger collection than before.—Mr. JouNaOERRTS (chairman of the Working- men's Committee), said he considered the statement which had just been read as on the whole satisfactory, but at the same time a deficiency in Keg leaked like going back instead of forward. He must say that the committee, of which he had been chairman for four years, had worked well, for if they had not the figures on the effiatement would never have been what they were. He oeuld, however, not help think- ing that there was a lot of work to he done yet by the-new committee. In looking over names of the firms who had no yet subscribed, he was sorry to say that they amounted to something like thirty. A part of these had subscribed in 1883, but since then they had fallen off. He could not ac- count for this except in the case of one firm which had given' him a reason that he thought at the time was a very proper reason, but he was pleased to say that this firm had again. commenced to subscribe, and he was quite sure that at end of 1885 the Infirmary would get from them some £3O or £4O. There was a quantity of smaller firms he considered ought to do something—from £3 to £5 each—which would be the means of bringing in over £lOO more thin what was got at the present time He sug- gested that these firms should be visited by tne new committee, and asked to organise a subscription. His experience was that weekly or monthly subscription greatly improved the subscriptions. He knew several firms that made weekly subscriptions, and the amount of subscriptions of these was more than three times what it used to be. He was confident that if effective steps were taken in this direc- tion the annual ;subscription would be increased £lOO or £l5O-Mr. W. A. ADAMS eunported these remarks of Mr. Roberts, and gave several instances to show the batter re- sults from organised weekly subscriptions.—Mr. AnatIYAWS confirmed the opinion of the last two speekers —Some dis- cussion next took place on a proposal of the Working-men's Committee to issue a list of the names of the firms which had subscribed, with the amounts of their subscriptions, also the names of those firms which had been asked to sub- scribe, but had not done so. It was ultimately agreed that this list should be publisheel.—Alderman DAVIES, having re— ferred to the manner in which the Infirmary was founded and to its objects, said he was obliged to say that there were many rich men who bad made all their money in 'Warring- ton, and who employed a great amount of labour—and labour was liable to accident—who gave little or nothing to its charitable institutions. (Hear, hear.) He o ten erieved about it, and he likewise grieved because- they would not only not do it themselves, but they took little or no interest in those who did assist and did their hest. He thought this class of people were not doing al+ duty to the society in which they lived. (Hear, hear.) This was a thing which might hereafter be a source of very great regret, as it might destroy that warm sympathy that ought to exist between class and class e Referring to the collectione at the churches, he said he thought that for £lB2 to be collect-ed at churches in the town in one day was very creditable indeed. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. AMANT3 said he was glad to hear the expressioas of Alderman Davies. He was himself of opinion that the shopkeepers and the " np;4er ten " had not subsclbed as they ought to do, and he thought the working-men present ought to express themselves strongly on the point. lie had looked through the report last year, and he found that many of the subecriptiens of these people did not amount to more than lett, 55, and even so low as 2.4 84 a year. The working-man who subscribed 14. a week gave 4e 41 a year. They ought to try to shame these men to do at least as much as the working-men, several of whom hid expressed themselves strongly that men who were living at ease should do so little. In con. elusion Mr. Adams suggested that if tradesmen did not con- tribute money they might subscribe in kind.—Alderman Davies said he had not alluded so much to shopkeepers. He thought they had rather a hard time of it, and that they did pretty well towards the Infirmary. He had meant the rich people who had made their fortunes in Warrington. t These penple did not give that scot of support to the insti• tution that they ought to do. This subject then dropped.— An execnt.ive committee' composed of the following, was appointed. viz.:—Messrs John Roberts, Joseph Potter, W. Adams, F. Browne, Thos. Armstronz, John Scattergood, Thos. Burton, John Willett, Robert Sutton, J. Hartley, J. Alcock, George Jones, John Taylor, Fowler, H. Darwin, and B. nudge. Mr. John Roberts was unanimously re-appointed chairman of this committee. Votes of thanks to the Mayor, Mr. Armitage, Mr. John Roberts, and to the medical men of the town, for their services in connectton. with the institution, brought the meeting to a close,
_GENERAL NEWS.

Two natives of India were called to the Bar in the Middle Temple on Monday. Mr Deasy, M P for Cork, has declared the Matadi to be a native of that city, stating his name to be Sullivan. It is stated that the Queen will leave England at the end of March, and remain on the Continent for three weeks. At a crowded meeting of Liberal electors of the Broughton Division of Salford on Wednesday night Mr. Arthur Arnold was unanimously selected as the Liberal candidate for the division at the general election. Mr. R. Leake, M.P., and Mr. W. Agnew, M.P., on Wed- nesday night addressed a public meeting at Ramsbottom, the former dealing with the foreign and the latter with the home policy of the Government. _

_ At the Cheshire Winter Assizes, on Wednesday, John Saunders, a letter sorter, employed in the Birkenhead Post- office, was sentenced to five years' penal servitude for stealing two letters containing valuables. Tuesday night's London Gazdte announces that at the Council at Osborne on Tuesday, Her Majesty declared her consent to a contract of matrimony between the Princess Beatrice and Prince Henry Maurice of Battenberg. At the instance of the London and North-Western Rail- way Company (owners of the Admiral Moorsom), the ship Santa Clara, lying in the Birkenhead Dock, has been "arrested," pending the company's action to recover dam- ages. -

MR. LABOUCHERE' M.P., MULCTED IN £1.,657.—At Bod- min Assizes, on Tuesday, an action brought by Messrs. Wil- Iyamsand Company,bankers, against Mr. Henry Labouchere, proprietor of Truth, was settled, the defendant consenting to a verdict for £1,657. Messrs Andrew Scott and Co.'s cotton mill in Glasgow was burned down on Wednesday. The operatives were at work when the fire broke out, and in the excitement of the exit a number of women were injured. The loss of property is estimated at £30,000. MARRIAGE Ow REV. STEPHEN GLADSTONE.—The marriage of the Rev. Stephen E. Gladstone, second son of the Premier and rector of Hawarden, with Miss Wilson, daugh- ter of Dr. Wilson, was solemnised on Thursday in Christ Courch, Liverpool, in the presence of a very large gathering of relatives, friends, and representatives of public bodies. The Prime Minister and Mrs. Gladstone were in attendance ' at the ceremony, and received an enthusiastic welcome from an enormous crowd which lined the streets near the church. FIRE IN ULASCOW.—FOUR PERSONS BURNT TO DEATH. It now transpires that four persons perished in the fire on Wednesday night, at the mills of Messrs. Andrew Scett and Co., Bridgeton, their names being Joseph Hart, aged 50; Mary Cranstone. 15; Mary Peden Mchlarg, 16; and Rose Ann Smith, 20. They entered the mill on Wednesday after- noon, and have not since been seen. Sarah Kennedy and Mary O'Neil, who are in the infirmary, the former with a broken leg and the latter severely burned, are doing well. MR. BRADLAUGR'S APPEAL.—In the Court of Appeal, on Tuesday, the argument on Mr. Bradlaugh's appeal wet re- sumed. The preliminily eltellone Of the Attorney- General Were disposed of in Nr. Bradlauglee favour, and the Attorney-General proceeded to show cause that the rule should not be made absolute. He contended tnat unless some tes'imonv were forthcoming to the meaning of the words "Solemnly and publicly subscribed," it would be Competent for Mr. Bradlaugh to subscribe the oath upon his shirt sleeve.—The Master of the Rolls said if the word in the Act had been " take " the oath it must have been ad- ministered, but the word was "make."—Mr. Bradlaugh was replying *hen the court rose. On Wednesday the Court gave judgment for the Crown, and Mr. Bradlaugh moved for stay of execution pending an appeal to the House of Lords. The Attorney-General did not oppose the appli- cation, and it was granted. INDUSTRIAL CONFERENCE—A Conference on the question of industrial remuneration, which was opened on Wednes- day in London, was attended by more than 100 delegates. Sir C. Duke, who presided, explained that the Conference consisted of representatives of the Statistical Society, cham- bers of commerce, associations of capitalists, delegates of trade unions, of econemic societies, and of fri-ndly societies, and that those who took part in the Conference belonged to both great parties in the State, and represented very vary- ing forms of opinion. Papers were read by Sir T. Brassey on cooperative induetry and industrial organisation, and by Mr. Lloyd Jones on the unequal distribution of wealth. A paper contributed by Mr. D. Cunningham, of Dundee, on the I question of wages and the cost of the nececsariee of life was taken as read, and an interesting discussion followed. On ' the reassembling of the Conference after a brief adjourn- ment, a paper was read by Miss Simeon on the loss or gain ' of the working classes, her contention being that it is true of the middle class as it is of the whole community that the rich in it are groeing richer and the poor poorer. Mr. W. Saunders contributed a paper in which he argued that the land system and the conduct of some landowners were wholly responsible for the poverty of the country. After a piper on skilled and unskilled labour in the shipbuilding trade there was considerable discussion, in the course of which Mr. Ball of the Agricultural Labourers' Union, de- clared that the rand question was at the root of the evils they had met to discuss. On Thursday the Conference ' eves resumed, under the presidency of Sir C. Dilke. The opening address was by Mr. I. Lowthian Bell, of the British Iron Trade Association. LIBERAL DEMONSTRATION AT BIRMINGHAM..—Mr. Bright and Mr. Chamberlain addressed their cmstituents at Bir- mingham on Thursday evening. Mr. Bright commenced by a congratulatory reference to the part taken by Birmingham and other large towns in the agitations which produced the Reform Acts of 1832 and 1807, and also that which bad just been passed. They had, he said, now thrown open the por- tals of the temple of freedom, and had invited not a classl but the nation to enter. Passing to the work before the re- formed Parliament, the right hon. gentleman, while admit- , Wog the practicability of legislation as regards disestablish- ' rnent in Scotland and Wales, said the question of dises.ab- Bailment in England was not ripe for any Cabinet likely to be seen during the coming Parliament. He believed this was a question which would work itself out without vio- lent attacks from the outside. The land question ought to receive the attention of the new Parliament. No queation ought to have precedenee of it. Oar ever growing empire was to his mind a delusion and a snare, and the idea of im- perial federation of which we had heard so much was ridicu- lous. He was for friendet4 and justice to all our colcnies and to foreign Powers, but thought we had enough on our hands.—Mr. Chamberlain,' who had a most enthusiastic welcome, referred in his opening remarks to the fate of the late Colonel Burnaby, whom he described as a courteous' political opponent, and as brave a soldier as ever wore the British uniform. The right hom gentlemen expressed his-, ' deep gratification that General Stewart had secured the main object of his mission, and trusted that when the res- cue of those in Khartoum was aoncraplished we should leave that country to lee governed alter the choice of its own ' people. He condemned the recant dynamite outrages in London, and said it was time for every honest man to raise his voice against those detestable proe-eedings. It was time I for Mr. Parnell, who had unequalled influence with his fel- low-countrymen, to s marate himself from those wicked crimes, not merely by silence, but by, denouncing them in • public. The bulk of Mr. Chamberlain's speech was occu- pied with a defence of his recent suggestions as to the cleanse of future Liberal policy under Democratic control. Ha again urged the necessity of someeinamediate reform in , the system of land tenure and in the conditions of life amongst the masses of population in large towns. SIR. ARTHUR ARNOLD, M.P., ON LAND REFORM.—A

. , mreting was held on Monday night at Leigh to hear an ad- dress on " Land Reform" by Mr. A. Arnold, M.l'.—fr. Arnold combatted Mr. Chamberlain's view that if we cheapened and facilitated the transfer of land and abolished the feudal laws and customs which led to its accumulation in so few hands the land would still remain with the same class of people. If he thought this view would turn out to be correct he would regard all their reforms as mere waste of time. His belief was that if the soil of'this country was free land it would pass largely to those who would cultivate it with their own bands. In other countries peasants had acquired a large proportion of the land Emcee they were prepared to give more for it than the rich cared to give. Here the reverse had been the case, but landowning on the English system had received a terrible shock, and already the ideal position was no longer thought, of. The great landowner landlords were suffering deeply, and now was the opportunity for the abolition of the stepid fiction that the people have no concern with the land. Let them not rest until they had established the truth that the land is the people's and the fnlness thereof. The d'stress and perplexity of the landlords came at the very moment when the power of the people was to be made absolute and supreme. He did not suggest that they should act in a revengeful spirit,though the pro- vocation had been great. He trusted that the landlords of this country would not seek a selfish remedy. If the land- lords wanted as a body to advocate plunder, of the people in order to maintain the rotten edifice of feudalism in this country, they would not deserve to be delivered from those advocates of absolute fixity of tenure and of free sale whom they ought to fear. For his part, he would hold out to them the rich promise of relief as the price of the ransom of the land. He would say, let our land be free as our trade is free, and you shall have wealth more abundant-than before. (IGive us free land, and you shall be first and foremost in reaping the advantages of that liberty. Freedom and free. don only will restore the value of your wasted estates. Let us join altogether in trampling down the immorality of the law of primogeniture. Let us have done at once and for ever with the pride, the vain glory, the folly, the injury of the system which per,nits that long_ after death a proprie- tor may control the destiny of the surlatee of the country. Let es get rid of the methods of conveyance and of mort- gage which are a burden and a disgrace to oar civilisation, such as no foreign Government would dare impose upon its people. Let us assert the truth that to deal promply by displacoment with a bankrupt landlord is even more needful for the interest of Commonwealth thark in the interest of a bankrupt trader. Lotus liberate the lifd. There never have ' '
bcen such imlucemenls to that noble work; then with free trade and free land we shall go forward certain of maia- taining our high place among the nations of to „

FOOTBALL. Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to thehead office, Bewsey-street, Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.

NICOL LANE V. STUBSHAW CROSS.—Played on Saturday on the Stubshaw Cross ground and resulted in a win for Nicol Lane by three goals to one. , ST. HELENS RECREATION V. HOUOIL—ThiS match was played On Saturday and resulted in a victory for St. Helens by one goal and two minor points to four minor points. VULCAN V. KIREDALE.—PIayed on Saturday on the ' ground of the first-named and resulted in a victory for the Vulcan team by one goal and two minor points to nil. HAYDOCIC RECREATION V. ASHTON RECREATION (IST Tuams).—This match was played on the ground of the lat- ter on Saturday. After a disagreeable game the visitors won by two goals to one disputed. LATCHFORD TRUE BLUES V. RUNCORN MERSEY MISSION. —Played on the ground of the latter on Saturday, and ended in a victory for Latchford by one goal and seven minor points to one minor point. Buckley and Davies played well for their respective sides.

_ WARRINGTON TRUE BLUES V. WIGAN ROVERS.—The re- turn match between the above clubs was played at Warring- ton on Saturday, and after a well contested game resulted in a win for the home team. Score: Warrington True Blues, one goal, two tries, one disputed try, seven minor points, to Rovers one minor point. WARRINGTON EXCELSIOR V. ST. BARNABAS (IST TEAR). —The return match between these clubs was played on the ground of the former on Saturday, and after a fast game resulted in a victory for the Excetsiors by one goal (dropped from the field by S. Jones) and five minor points, to one try and two minor points. All the Excelsior for wards I played well, while Jones and Hackett were seen to advan- tage at the bask. The try for the visitors was obtained by Parker, of the White Star, the attempt at goal by Allton being unsuccessful.

ST-. PETER'S (NEWTON) V. SUNDAY SCHOOL TEACHERS.— An enjoyable afternoon was spent by the teachers and scholars connected with St. Peter's Sunday school, Newton, on Saturday. A match at football was played on the Mesnes between the Newton St. Peter's club and the Sun- day school teachers, and a pleasant game resulted in favour of the latter by three goals to two. At the invitation of Mr. W. Haskell, one of the teachers, the players and a few friends sat down to tea in the school-room. Hearty votes of thanks were afterwards expressed to Mr. Hatkell for his kindness. RAYDOCK TEMPERANCE V. HAYDOCK ST. JAMES'S—Con- siderable interest was manifested in the meeting of these teams on the ground of the Temperance club, near the Wagon and Horses, Haydock, on Saturday afternoon, and there was a large attendance of spectators. The Temperance melt played with the wind in the first half, and had the best of the play, but half time was called before either team had scored, On the change 9f ends till kaMS was fast, and both elevens exerted themselves 10 Secnrs it leading point. The home eleven ultimately scored, and as this was the only point of the match the result was a victory for the Tem- perance by one goal to nil. • RUNCORN RECREATION V. LIVERPOOL MONTROSE.—On Saturday the Recreations journeyed to Liverpool to meet the above club for the first time. The Malcom captain winning the toss, decided to play with the wind and slightly uphill. In a short time the R.creations obtained a touch- in-goal, On kick out, play was kept up in neutral ground until close on half time, when the Montrose were forced to save. After change of sides the Recreations were hardly pressed several times, but by some good play on the loose the forwards rushed the ball back to their oppments' goal, and Clare nicely got over the line, fr.,ln which he added the major point. Close on time the Recreations gained another touchdown, and left the field victors by one goal and three minor points to nil.

Rut-Toms v. MOSSLEY.—This return fixture was played at Runcorn on Saturday. The visitors arriving very late, a game of only 40 minutes' duration WAS Dlayed, when fdossley scored a try, two minor points, to Runcorn two minor points. England gained the try. The game was stubbornly contested, the home team having none of the worst of it, fo-cing Rylance to kick dead on two occasions. Teams :--,,ltuncorn : Hughes, back ; Speakman, Wain- wright, and H Hughes, three-quarter backs ; Wright and Andrews, half-backs ; Cox, Lewis, licffland, Clarke, Than, Barns, Cliff, Joule, and Gatley, forwards. Massie,- : Rylance, back ; Newby, Lawton, and England, three-quar- ter backs ; Billings and Winterbottom, half-hacks ; Ash- worth, Firth, Howard, Mayall, Mortared, Makin, Rowan, and Wadsworth, forwards. WARRINGTON V. WlGAN.—Pliyed at Warrington on Saturday, and resulted in a victory for the home team by one goal, one try, and ten minors to Wigan nil, Gilbert opened the game, Duddle replying. The play settled in Wigan terri ory. Making the most of this advantage. Barnes shot for goal, a minor being the result. Morris afterwards got the ball away, but the Warrington forwards, by good combined play, again threatened, and Turter made a bold bid for a drop goal. Minors at this point were quickly scored. On change of ends a mis-judged pass by Morris to Slavin let in Turner, who gained Warrington quarters. Pressing onwards, Warrington again forced their opponents to save. Wigan could not free their goal for any definite time, when at this juncture Success crowned the efforts of Barnes, who dropped the oval over the cross-bar for quarter flag. The visitors' goal was once more assailed, and by sterling play Rigby got over near touch Griloert was com- pelled to retire owing to -an accident. Up to the call of tune Wigan were certainly outplayed. Teams :—Warring- ton : Back, T. Walsh ; three-quarter backs, J. T. Massey, Speakman, and E. Gilbert; forwards, H. Ashton (captain), F. Turner, W. Hayes, W. Povey, J. Jolley, T. Davies, J. Robinson, W. Dillon, and J. Rigby. Wigan: Back, Norris; three•quarter bides, J. Slavin, paddle, and F. Finney; half- backs, Morris and Bancks ; forwards, Holt (captain), Bray- shay, Prestt, Ingham, Astley, Matthews, Mockett, Cavey, and Underwood.

LIVERPOOL AND DISTRICT CuP TIE. EARL OWN WANDERERS V. GOMBORNE —Over 1000 persons assembled on the ground of the Wanderers' club, at Earlestown, en Saturday afternoon, to witness the meeting of the Earles• town Wanderers and Got borne first teams in the third round of the competition for de Liverpool and District Associa- tion Challenge Cup. The supporters of the respective teams manifeeted some encitement, and occasionally high words were indulged in. Shortly before three o'olock the players appeared in the field in the following order :—Wan- derers : T Champion, goal ; H Selby and W Lord, backs; Ef Johnson, J Lowe, and W half-backs ; F Koowles and T Thompson, right wing; W Dale, centre ; J Shaw and W Shaw, left wine- ; umpire, C Walker. Golborne : W Jenkinson, goal ; eßate and J Waddington, backs ; P Ridyard, J Clarke, and T Kay, half-backs ; A Allen and S Morris, right wing ; 6 Cottarn, centre; R Hemborouela and J Clare, left wing • umpire, I' Herrick ; referee, Mr Manners, Liverpool. the Golleerne team won the toss end for the first half chose to play with the ground and wind in their favour. Dale started the leather for the Wanderers, and for a few minutes the play was of an even character. Owing to tniskicks on the part of the Earlestown backs the visitors forvrertis had one or two chances of ecorine but Champion cleverly saved his charge. After about twenty minutes' playa scrimmage occurred in front of the Earle:- town uprights, and Champion missed the leather, but Lord kicked it away from under the bar, and it was sent up the field. The visitors claimed that the ball had been through the posts, and amid the cheers of the Golborne supporters the referee allowed the point, which turned out to be the only goal of the match. Up to the change of ends the play was very fast, and ends were changed with the scare Golborne-, one ; Wanderers, none. On the resumption of the game Earlestown strove hard to secure an equalising point, and several times the Golborne posts were seriously endangered. The leather could not be forced between, how- ever, andwhen time was called, Golborne were declared the winners by one geal to none. The Wanderers objected to the goal, and brought the matter, in the form of a protest, before the notice of the -committee of the Liverpool and Dis- trict Association, It came up for consideration at a meet- ing of the committee at Liverpool on Tuesday evening, and after hearing the statements of the we umpires and re- feree, and representatives of the two clebs, the committee upheld the objection, and ordered the game to be re-played at Golborne.

and the heaviest fire sustained. Colonel Sir C. Wilson, as senior officer, assumed the command. Wile force, leaving thQ wounded and impedimenta in a work construcied under heavy fire, marched about 3 p.m. on the 19th inst. on the gravel ridge overlooking the Nile, whcre a large force of the enemy was established. The enemy charged, led by several Emirs on horse• back, but none were able t get nearer to the square than about thirty yards. They were repulsed with heavy loss. Five Emirs and about 250 dead were left on the ground. Their wounded were very numerous. Sir C. Wilson, in his report, says nothing could exceeed the coolness of the troops, both when exposed to the fire of the sharpshooters in the morning, and to the charge of spearmen in the afternoon. He speaks highly of Colonel Boscawen, to whom he gave com- mand of the square during the operations on the 2rst. .

- A reconnaissance in force was made on Metem- meh, which has been placed in a state of defence and walls loopholed. Although Sir C. Wilson reports he could have carried the village ,which is long and strag• gling, he did not think it worth, the loss it would have entailed. On the 22nd inst. a reconnaissance was made down the river towards Shendy, with three steamers, which returned the same day. I most deeply deplore the losses we have experi- enced, but in every other respect the . result of these operations so ably and successfully conducted by Sir Herbert Stewart is most satisfactory, and cannot fail to have a great effect upon the future of this campaign. I have had no letter of any importance from General Gordon, the most recent, dated 29th Dec., contains merely one line saying, "Khartoum all right; could hold out for years. Sir R. Buller starts to-morrow to assume the com- mend alone. the desert route to Gubat. We have plenty of troops, ammunition, and food. The Royal Irish begin their movements across the desert to-day; the West Kent will follow. Sir Herbert Stewart writes in good spirits from on board one of the steamers. The latest report of him says he is doing well; but his wound is very severe, and I cannot expect him to .be fit for any more work this campaign. The temporary deprivation of his services at this moment I regard as a national lose. Ha is one of the ablest soldiers and most dashing commanders I have ever known. I recommended him most strongly to the Queen for her Majesty's most favourable con- sideration. I append a list of the killed and wounded. I regret to saw that Lord St. Vincent and Lieutenant Guthrie, of tha Royal Horse Artillery, have died of their wounds. The only officers killed since the 17th are Quartermaster Lima, rsth Hussars, and Con- ductor Jewell. .
The enemy die not flAt with the same determina- tion or courage as on the r7th inst.
THE QUEEN'S- CONGRATULATIONS.

Her Majesty has telegraphed her congratulations to Lord Wolseley on the success which has attended General Stewart's advance, at the same time expressing her sympa- thy with the wounded and her regret at the loss of so many valuable lives. Her Majesty has aho teleFraphed to Lady Stewart, complimenting her on Sir Hertkrt Stewart's gallant achievement and expressing a hope for his speedy recovery. Liter information received by Lady Stewart states that her distinguished husband is progressing satisfactorily.

RECEIPT OF THE NEWS AT THE WAR OFFICE. The long-expected news of Sir Herbert Stewart and the little farce which went forward from Abu Klea on the 18th inst. towards Metemrneh was received in London and the provinces on Wednesday morning with unbounded satisfac- tion. The growing anxiety for intelligence was manifested at an early hour in the forenoon, when the first intimation leaked out from the War Office that despatches had been received from Lord Wolseley. The rumour spread with extraordinary rapidity, and within an incredibly short time Pall Mall contained an eager and excited stream of inquirers directed towards the War Office, where, before long, the visitors congregated in num- bers far too large for the authorities to attend to. Mes- sengers from the clubs and the other Government departments, officers on leave, and others, flocked in crowds to the War Office, the excitement being heightened by the shouting of the vendors of early editions of the evening newspapers, containing rumours that Metamrneh had been taken, and Goner tl Stewart wounded. DETAILS OF THE FIGHT.

Lord Wolseley's despatch, though lengthy, gives few details of the fighting, but from this telegram and other accounts which have reach.td London from Korti and Cairo, it would appear that Sir Herbert Stewart, after leaving a strong guard at Abu Klea Wells in charge of the men who were wounded in the engagement of the 17th, went forward on the evening of the followin r day with a force of a little over one thousand men and a large number of camels towards Metetnineh, with the object of pro- fling by the route of the Mihdi's Arabs to occupy that place. The advance appears to have been made but slowly, for, although Itletemmeh is only about 23 miles from Abu Klea, the forcs only reached that place on the morning of the 19th. Sir tierlArt Stewart and his Camel Brigade crossed the rough valley and subsequent sandy plains which are characteristic of tie camel route from Abu Klea to Metemmeh, and, leaving the Shahacat Wells on their left, proceeded towards the Nile.

About seven o'clock on the morning of the 19th, what about three or four miles from the river, the enemy was sighted in force, and the British halted and cons'ructed z treba, behind which breakfast was served out under a heavy fire from the enemy. It was at this tirus thlt a shot from the enemy disabled General Stewart, and Sir C Wilson, as senior officer, assumed the command. Leaving the wounded ami impediments in the zireba. our troops marched out about three p.m. in square against the enemy, now aacr. tamed to be 7,000 strong. The enemy charged brwely, led by several Emirs on horseback, but such was the effect of the British fire that none of them were able to approach within thirty yards of the square. Many of the enemy were armed with rifles, and they had a number of cavalry. They were ultimately re-

The fourth round of the English Cup competition was concluded on Saturday. Blackburn Rovers, Queen's Park, and Church had previously tattled their ties and Notts Forest and Notts County beat the London S wilts and Wel- sail Swifts. Old Etonians beat Middlesborough, and the Druids, after journeying to West Bromwich, were beatma by the Albion by 1 goal to nil. Lower Darwen had a journey to London, and at the close were pointless to Chatham 1 goal; the Lancashire club protest, that the referee called time four minutes too soon, and the Englis'A Association Committee will have to settle this. FATAL FIGHT AT WARRINGTON. Early on Sunday morning a man named William Lay- and, over fifty years of age, a bricksetter, of 8, Heath-lane, died under singular circumstances. His illegitimate daugh- ter, Ann Jane Kendall, was standing at the corner of Heath- lane and Golberne-street, engaged in conversation with William Gibbons, her sweetheart, a cellarman employed at the Barley Mow public-house' when deceased came to them and some angry words passed. A scuffle ensued, and Ley- land soon afterwards died in his house. Sabsequently Gib- bons was arrested, and on Monday morning he was brought before the Mayor and Mr. John Fairclougle, at the Borough Court, and charged with causing the death of William Ley- land by striking him en the head with his fist. Chief-con- stable Hunt stated the facts of the case as so far ascertained. He remarked that the prisoner, whe resided in Elizabeth- street, was about 22 years old, and his sweetheart was is. When the two were talking together at tha end of Golborne- streea on Saturday night, or early on Sunday mornine, Mrs Leylend, the girl's mother, went to them and said that it was time the girl went borne. Kendall replied "We have just got here ' • he has just left his work." Deceased heard the talking and went outside. Mrs Leyland alleged that when her husband came up to them Gibbons said to him "I have it in for you," but, on the other hand, the girl Ken- dall said that Gibbons did not make that remark, and that the deceased pushed against and struck her lover, alter which they had a scuffle and both fell on the ground.—? C 25 (Corbett). separated them, and deceased went home, afterwards dying whilst in the act of sitting down in an arm chair. He did not then purpose to call evideec' e but asked for a remand, pending the coroner's inquiry. Pri- soner was consequently remanded, the bell of his em- ployer, Mr Gleave, in £2O, being accepted. He had no report against Gib- bone, who appeared te be sober. The Coroner, in summing up, stid that if the jury were satisfied that Leylands died in consequence of something done by Gibbons, it was homicide. The next question wee whether it was justifiable or unlawful. Before they could say that it was justifiable they must be satisfied that the man ingicting the blow did everything he could to escape, be- fore strilling his opponent in self defence. They must be satisfied that Gibbons fled from impending danger, and that he Was unable to gain safety without retaliating and strik- ing Leyland. After a discussion in private, the jury returned a ver- dict of " manslaughter" against Gibbons. The Coroner offered to accept bail, Gibbons in MOO, and two sureties of £5O each. YESTERDAY'S MAGISTERIAL PROCEEDINGS. The accused man Gibbons was brought before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) at the Borough Police Court, yester- day, and charged on remand with causing the' death of Leyland. After the evidence given at the inquest had beem repeated with but little variation, the magistrate remarked that it was exceedingly contradictory, and that in his opinion Leyland's death was an accident. He did not think prieoner had the least intention of killing the unfortunate man. Mr. H. B. White, magistrates' clerk, expressed a similar opinion, and prisoner VMS discharged, Mr. A. Browne, by whom he was again represented, remarking that it was very improbable that a true bill would be returned against Gibbons by the Grand Jury, when he was indicted at the Assizes on the Coroner's irquiaition.

--------------------------------- Sir,—The Warrington Chamber of Commerce has issued Its eighth annual report. In this report I tir.l the follow- inz :—" The present rate of 3e. 91 per ton for iron, class A, 'Warrington to Liv-rpool and Birkenhead, will be reduced to 3s. 4d. per ton, station to elation, 2 ton lots." As this • reluction i 3 not intended to affect the large export ship- ments, sty 20, 30,50, or 100 ton patois, it is practically no benefit to manufacturers. If a redaction noon large export , Into had been secured, a substantial advantage would have been conferred upon the manufacturers of Warrington. As ' , the matter stands the concession is so trifling as not to deserve publication. I may state that the reduction an- nounced will not benefit the large concern with which lam connected to the extent of £1 per annum.—Yours faith- S. Warrineon, Jan. 26th, 1.885.

TRINITY CLOCK. Sir,—With a vi ;w to increase public cOnfidence in our 'new town clock. I send you a brief account of its recent performances. It use just accomplished a run of six weeks without any interference, and without getting more than a Tauter of a minute wrong during the time. Since August its errors have been oftener under than over a quarter of a minete, and have very rarely excedert half a minute. During the week, November 14th to 21st, it did not vary Mere than one second, according to the Leigh time signal, which 13 very reliable; I may here Paint out that the clock is set no that the first stroke of the hours shall give the correct time (the quarters being fire to seven seconde faster). and I would urge those who require the exact time of the clock to go by the strike Only. Tee dials of a turret clock can only be considered to indicate the time approximately, for reasons which must be sufficiently obvious to every one. In some cases dials are ,entirely dievneed with, as at Worcester and Chester Cathedrals. I can fancy cert,in individuals always ready ; to find fault, reminding me that the striking of the quar- ters was wrong on several occasions during the past year. ' These errors, however, as I subsequently ascertained, were net due to any fault in the clock, and might have been prevented with care, In future it is to be hoped that Mr. .J.Ym Croffleld's valuable gift will be anpreciated as it deserves. MONSTRATOR.

_ • HATDOCI LOcat, Bon.—The monthly meeting of this Beard was held on Monday afternoon, when there were present Messrs. O. Pilkington (in the chair), W. Balharry, J. Jackson, W. Alker, J. Cunliffe, W. Greenall, T. Turnbull (clerk), and Dr. Watkins (medical officer of health).—The Ziedical Officer's Annual Report: Dr. Watkin's :sad his report for the year 1884, which stated that there were regis- tared during the year in the township—births, 106 males 132 females, total 238; deaths, 48 miles 58 females, total 106. Excess of births over deaths, 58 males 74 females, total 132. There had been a remarkable absence of scarlet fever, but there was vet no provision for isolating cases of infections diseasa.—The Chairman rdmarked that the Board had not been idle in trying to do what they could to isolate cases of infectious disease. They had had communication with St. Helens and Warrington authorities, but nothing had yet been definitely decided.—After sims further remarks, Mr. Cunliffe expressed the opinion that each mem- ber of the Board should have an opportunity of considering the medical officer's report, and moved that it be left over until the next meeting of the Board.—Mr. Jackson seconded this motion, which was adopted —The Proposed New Rail- Mr. Goldsworth (surveyor) attended to confer with the Board with respect to the proposed new railway from St. Helene to Lowton, and which passes through the Haydock township. The report of Mr. Goldsworth (a summary of which has previously appeared in these columns) was con- sidered at some length; and it was decided to call a special meeting of the Board to pass a resolution opposing the scheme, or otherwise, on the 11th February next.— Finances: Accounts amounting to £BO 1.2 s 61 were ex- amined and passed for payment. —This was the principal business.

THE ELECTION OF A. GULRDIAN FOR NEWTON.=—The vacancy in the representation of Newton township on the Board of Guardians of the Warrington Union has this week been filled, but the name of the elected t.it'uarditn will not bo declared until to-night (Saturday). As stated last week, there were five candidates nominated, viz, John Clarke, ironmonger, Bridge-street, Earlestown ; Thomas Kilshtw, Cross-lane, gentleman; Joseph Pennington, farmer and builder, Winwick ; George Ratcliffe, 75, Sankey-street, Earlestown, gentleman; and James Sankey, wheelwright, High-street, Newton. Since the nominations were handed iv, Mr. Clarke, the adopted candidate of the anti-vaccina- time party, has withdrawn from the contest, but each of the four remaining gentlemen decided to go to the poll. There are about 2.000 voters in the township. Under the direc- tions of Mr. J. C. Sutton, clerk to the Guardians, 1,037 voting papers were delivered en Thursday to those entitled to vote, and were collected on Fri Jay. To-day (Saturday) Mr. Sutton, as returning officer, will proceed to count the votes given for each candidate, and will afterwards duly declare who has been elected.

LOCAL DYNAMITE SCARE.—Aa amusing scare occurred in) Warrington on WednesdAy morning. A person, evi- dently an Irishman, called at the Packet House Inn, Bridge Foot, kept by Mr. Clare, and there left a small parcel, in sdza about six inches by four, addressed to a farmer residing in the neighbourhood, and which was to be called for. The landlord took in the parcel in perfect good faith, and left it in the bar. Meanwhile his son, hearing something ticking in the parcel, called attention to it, and the idea was at ONCE) conceived that it conttined an infernal machine. The son seizad it and threw it into the middle of the street, and for a few moments consternation prevailed, the people in the vicinity decamping with all speed. The attention of a borough constable was called to the suspicions package, axd e, as it ivas abont to be thrown into the river close by, took the trouble to open it, revealing the contents to be a - couple of watches, both in motion.

Tnx °nun QIIESTION.-A preliminary meeqng for the furtherance of the Society for the Suppression of the Opium Trade was recently held in the St. Helens Town Hall under the presidency of the Mayor (Alderman Cook). Many of the local clergy were present. The Rev. Barrett, B.A ,of Liverpool. and Mr. W. H. Cooke, honorary secretary to the Liverpool auxiliary of the Society, gave addresses condemnatory of the trade, and explained the evils that arose from it. The Mayor expressed the opinion that the iniquitous traffic should be put an end to as soon as possible. After other gentlemea had briefly spoken, it was resolved unanimously that a public meeting on the question should be held during tee next few weeks. Votes of thanks to the deputation and tbe Mayor brought the pro- ceedings to a close.

A Row aT SITITON.—At the St. Helena Town Hall on Monday, before Messrs W. Pilkington and W. Blinkhorn, Daniel Channerly, of Swum, was summoned for assaulting James Stephens on the 27th December. The defendant, for whom Mr. J. 0. Swift awaeared, pleaded not guilty. The complainant stated that an the date named he and the de- fendant visited the Grapes Inn, Ecclestatt-lane Ends, and had drink together. They afterwards went to the complain.nt's house. where they had some more drink. When the complainant asked the defendant to leave, the latter violent- knocked him down against a box, and pressing his hands gainst the complainant's neck exclaimed, "I've got you now, and I'll be the death of you." The defendant after- wards struck him on the noso.—Mr. Swift, in defence, stated ,bat the parties were old friends, and after going on the • spree" together, they hid a quarrel.—The Bench thought Ihe affair Lad merely bten a drunken quarrel, ad trdered he defeadapt to pay the costs.

div.head: WARRINGTON WESLEY AN TEMPER-
div.p: WARRINGTON WESLEY AN TEMPER-
ANCE SOCIETY.

On Tuesday evening a meeting was held under the auspices of the above society, in Bold-street Wesleyan Se..oolroom. The chair was occupied by the Rev. J. Mc.Turk. and there were also present on the platform—Sir Wm. Fore M.A., K.O.M.G. ex-premier of New Zealand ; Mr. J. H. Raper, the Rev. J. 11. Jones, Mr. H. J. Guest, and Mr. It. Garnett. There was a good attenlance.—The CHAIR- MAN said it was a great gratification to many of them to be present at the first temperance meeting held in that now room. They had already dedicated that room to the work of Sunday-school teaching; they thought that the time I had come when they ought to dedicate it also to the tem- perance work in that town. (Applause.) There were many things transphing at the present day that gave them assur- ance that the cause they had at heart was making some progress. Such a speech as woe made at Bury the other day by the Attorney-General, Sir Henry James, would set before the conntry anew the fact that there were not only good times coming,-but that better times, had alrenty come. The Attorney-General showed in that able speech that daring the last Myears there had been a great diminution in the crimes of the first order that had been committed in this country. In 1864 the sentences to penal servitude numbered some 2800; in 1884 they numbered about half that number. (Ilear,..hear.) When he (the Attorney-Gene- ral) considered that there had been during that time an in- creasing population, he could only account for the diminution of crime and for the advance in sobriety and in the general welfare of the people by the fact that there had been carried on elementary education upon a scale that this country had had not before known, and that there had been going on at the same time a very vigorous effert to spread temperance principles. (Applause.) He was very grateful that these matters were being noted by those in the high places of our land, and set so effectively before the country. Let them be grateful that so far they had won seine victories, tut let them also, and especially those of them who were in- terested in the church conuected with than hall, resolve that they would throw their whole force into that movement to nary it somewhat further and to make it of greater benefit to this nation. (Ateplause.)—Mr. R. Garnett moved " That this meeting recognising the great moral, social, and physi- cal evils originating in Intemperance, rejoices in the success vouchsafed by Providence to the temperance reformation, and hereby resolves to aid the efforts which are made on be- half of total abstinence from the use of intoxicating liquors, and the enactment of laws applying a direct popular veto on the sale of liquces." (Applause.)—Mr. RAPER seconded this resolution. They were, he said, about to have a tem- perance society in connection with that hall, which would cover all the phases of the temperance reformation. It would almost occupy an evening to describe the various departments of that deeply intereeting movement called temperance re- formation. That reformation was only a movement of the present day, for some of them were just now celebrating from time to time its jubilee. It was not often that they were under such circumstances as to be able to look backwards over the history of' a movement of that kind. Some 'of the very earliest workers belonged to this very neighbourhood. Light travelled slowlyo and scientific and moral truths outside the Bible also.travelled slowly,and there were men and Women to-day who could not for a moment contemplate with any sitisfaction any censure on the use of intoxicating liquors, because they knew a number of very exc-Ilent men and women who were both drinkers, drink- makers, and drink-sellers. They could not o ,nceive for a mcraent that all these practices of early times could be con- sidered inconsisttnt with the light they had at the present moment. But it must be borne in mind that they were privileged to receive revelations continually. The advance of physical science alone brought with it great responsibility. They had also the light of this latter part of the 19th cen- tury manifested in Donning-street when Mr. Gladstone sent an invitation to Lord Saliebury and Sir Stafford Nortbcate to come and take a cup of tea, and they settled the whole reform question. (Laughter and applause.) The speaker then remarked that there had been a great increase of light in recent years as to the nature of alcohol, owing to their tak- ing the advice of Lord Bacon and questioning nature on the subject. Every answer that came from nature was that alcohol waa a brain poison, and he bad no heeitation in

Mr. Gladstone and the Marquis of Hartington arrived at Cark station on the Furness Railway yesterday afternoon, on a visit to the Duke of Devonshire at Hollrer Hall. The Premier was in good health, and his visit is expected to last several days, THE ALLEGED MOCK MARRIAGE.—At Chester on Friday Thomas Pugh, labourer, and Thomas Stevens, accountant, I charged with conspiring to perform a mock marriage be- tween Pugh and a young wornaa named Mary Emma It arris, were acquitted. A conference on peace and international art-dtration, in connection with the Peace Society, was held on Friday afternoon, at Darlington. Sir Joseph Pease, M P, presided, and the speakers 'included Mr Hy, Richard, M I', and Sir Hy Havelock Allen. ham OF a STRIKE.—After lasting nearly 23 weeks, the serious strike of colliers at the Elm and Miesygreig pits, Buckley, Flintshire, has coma to a termination by the men conceding to the masters' demands, and on Monday the col- liens will again be in full swing. The following notification appears in last night's Gazette: —"War Offioe,'2o.h January. Tom ?I/amt.—An inqu.?st on Mr. ;Toni Naih, barrier, fennd dead in his chambers in the Temple, London, on Wednesday, with a revolver in his hand, was held on Friday at the White Swan, Temple-street. Evi- dence showed deceased had recet.tly suffered under the de- lusion that his constitution was breaking up, and that he was unable to cope with his work. A verdict of " Suicide whilst in a state of temporary ins " was returned. MURDER OF a Mornna.—At Wormesgay On Friday, a young man named Everitt rose from his bed and proceeded In his mother's bedroom and attacked her with a knife; in- flicting such terrible injuries that the poor woman died shortly afterwards. Everitt, who was immediately arrested, always appeared to be fond of his mother. He is supposed to be of weak intellect.
TEIE DYNAMITE CONSPIRATORS: IMPORTANT
ARREST.

The Central News states: We have every ream to believe, although the police authorities absolutely refuse to give any information on the subject-, that an important arrest, having a direct bearing op ut the recent dynamite outrages, was effected on Friday morning in London. A , fortnight ago a rum giving the name of Goodman hired a furnished bark parlour in North-st„ Westminster, arrang- ing to pay 5s di per week rent. He stated that he came from Notting Hill. He brought a large box with him, paid his rent in advance, and was provided with a latch key. lie never bad any visitors, nor did he receive any letters until Friday. He kept good hours, cnly occasionally going out for a short time in the evening, and was quiet and steady in his demeanour. The landlady saw so little of him that she is able to describe him with difficulty. As far, however, as she can state with reasonable c,rtainty, he was tall, had a small dark brown moustache, and wore a long dark loose overcoat. The landlady does not think he had any whiskers. Goodman went out early on F‘iday morningaemmking to his landlady that he would be leaving her that day. Apparently, his intention was to fetch a cab, but he evidently noticed that the house was being watched, for he quickly re-entered the house. Shortly afterwards he was arrested, and it is also under- stood that the box is in the possession of the police. Tae Central News has ascertained that tha house has been watched for some days past. •

THE SOUDAN CAMPAIGN.-400 ARAB HORSEMEN
KILLED.

-------- A Morning Post telegram from Korti states :—The 'Jody of 600 Arab horse who charged our square was crempletely annihilated, the nearest spot to the square at which one of their dead was found being 50 yards from our line. The Pall Mall Gazette says. the next news from Me- tarnmeh will probably be brought across the Desert by Sir C. Wilson, who will desire to confer with Lord Wolsekv after ascertaining the views of General Gordon. We ought to have General Gordon's views and Sir C. Wilson's report on the state of Khartoum early next week. It is added that General Gordon's diary was handed to Sir C. Wilson on the 21st, at Gubat.

PARK LANE VILLAGE CLUB AND PARLIAMENTAK3 DE- BATING SoctEnr.—This club celebrated their annual tea party on Saturday, Over 100 persons.sat down to a good re- past. After tea an entertaioment was arranged. Mr. C. F. Clark (president) presided. Mr. John Robinson (secretary) read a report on the working of the club during the past 12 months. Its financial position bad improved, and the present number of members was 120. If the good spirit, kindly feeling, and respect for each other's political core- victions only continued, he ventured to predict a bright future for the club. On the motion of the Rev. Geo. FO -22 seconded by Mr. Samuel Woods, a vote of thanks was ac- corded to Mr. Clark for the support he had accorded to the- dab.

The Arrinertoss OF FOOTBSZL —On Friday, at the. Wigan County Police Court, twe summonses arising eut of offences committed under the Mines Regulation Act were. heard.—E iward Conroy, furnaceraaa at No. 3 pit of the Pewfal I Col liery,.Ashton, belonging to Messrs. R. Evan and 1 Company, was summoned for neglecting to carefully attend to the furnace in his charge, and for leaving the same be- fore the night furnaceman came; and John Simm, engine- man, was summoned for not preventing one George t•trone, a person not employed therein, from going down the pit, contrary to the special rules.--Mr. J. a Swift (St. Helens) prosecuted, and said it was Simm's duty to be at the en• glees on the pit bank, to lower people down and wind them up the pit. On the 6th December he was on duty at the engines, and the defendant Conroy was the only person down the pit. Simm then told him he was anxious to see a football match, an asked him if would leave his furnace. Conroy, too good naturedly perhaps said he wonld, and he left the furnace to take care of itself from ten minutes to three until the night furnaceman came at six o'clock.— Conroy said he simply obeyed the engineman, and Simm pleaded guilty. The summons against Conroy was dis— missed, and Simm was fined 40s and casts.

He also mentioned that in the temperance hospital that had been instituted 25,000 had been dealt with without any aid from alcoholic liquors ; and that the dangerous character of alcohol was very clearly shown by the figures of a life-insurance society they had. They had calculated that during the last 17 years teetotal members ought to have died to the ' number of 2,879; but instead of that °Ply 2,035 had died, leaving 844 still alive (applause) and out of 4,741 moderate drinkers who wern due to die. 4,640 did die, leaving only 101 alive. (Hear, hear.) Torough the abstainers not dying--(laueiter)—there was saved £lBB,OOO which was dividedout as hotlines amongst the teetotallers every five years. (Applause.)—Sir Fox, in suppoitin,-; the resolution, referied to the speeches of Mr Chimberlain and Sir Charles Dilke on the temper- ance question. From the remarks of those gentlemen, be said, it seemed that it was proposed to hand twee the licen- sing powers which the magistrates now possessed to the corporate bodies in towne,,and to the bodies which would be created in counties by Mr Trevelyan's proposed bill. This was not what Sir Wilfrid Lawson intended, and tem- perance-bodies had protested very strongly against it. There was another method of which he bad been a witness. It was that the licensing pow,..r should be vested in a licensing bench elected by the-people for that special purpose. In his county this system had been tried for three years, and dur- ing that time there had only been one drink shop stopped out of their 2,200. At this rate it would take 6,600 years to , get rid of the whole system. (Laughter.) He supported the plan by which each elector would have the opportunity of directly saying by his vote whether or not he would have drink shops in his locality. (Applause.) Ho conclu- ded by referring to the reliiious aspect of the temperance nvestion.—Substqueatly a committee for the Wesleyan . Temperance Society was formed, and the chairman and secretary appointed. Votes of thanks were paasel to the speakers.

ACCIDENT.—On Saturday evening, when the streets ware crowded, a woman was knocked down in Horsemarket-street by a horse and trap, but received no injuries beyond:a shaking. NARROW ESCAPE AT THE CENTRAL STATION.—..On Wed- neaday a very narrow escape occurred at the Central Sta- tion. Mr. Pargeter, generally known in the neighbourhood as " Hippy Jim," an auctioneer, was crossing the line, when he slipped aad fell. A. train was in motion in the station.at the time, and Mr. Pargeter was in imminent danger, when two of the railway officials dragged him away as the engine was close upon them. A RASCAL PITNISRED,—The Borough Magistrates on Mon- I day sent a youth nanted William Farrell to jail for six months for beating his mother, who told the Court that on tho 17th lust he struck her several times, knocked her down, and kicked her. In passing sentence, the Mayor regretted that he was unable to order him to be lashed, remar:Ang that if he could order fifty lashes to b 9 inflicted upon him he would take that course. _

HOLY TRINITY CIIIII;CH SOIREE..—On Tuesday evening a well attended soiree was held in connection with, this church in the school room, Museum-street, which wns de- corated for the occasion. Tea having been served,in the early pirt of the evening, a varied programme was subse- quently gone though by rnembers of the choir and several friends. Songs and readings were given, and a musical medley, entitled the 4. Nursery," conclutkd the programme. Mr. W. Johnson, organist at Holy Trinity, acted as accompanist.

A HEARTLESS FATHER.— At the Borough Court, on Saturday, Michael Fogarty, a powerfully-built man, a pad- dler, last from Manchester but a native of hiraerick, was charged in custody with leaving his two children chargeable to the Warrington Union. From a statement made by Mr Shearer, relieving officer, it appeared that prisoner had been several times previously convicted. Since 1880 he has done little or no woi k, and has cost the ratepayers over £llO for the maintenance nf himself and two, children. He was committed as an incorrigible rogue to take his trial at the next Quarter Sessions.

- INCORRIGIBLE.—John Lee, a boy, was charged at the Boroagh Court on Welnesday, with having stolen a snit of clothes, value 20e, the property of William Shepherd, labourer, of 53 Eldon-street, by whom ho had been adopted. The plutons day Shepherd went to work, and returning at breakfast tin, discovered that his adopted child had disap- peared with the suit of clothes. The police were communi- cated with, and it was found that the boy had been trying to dispose of the suit. Prisoner, who has before heel) in trouble, was sent to prison for a month, to be follev€Ab.v five years' detention in a rafonnate,ry.

The accompanying map will explain the route taken by General Stewart, the places at which the recent battle have been fought, and the.position of the troops ascending the Nile to the relief of General Gordon. Our map gives in detail the great bend of the Nile which takes place about 100 miles north of Khartoum, and from the sketch the reason will be apparent of the desert march of General Stewart, which has alretdy resulted in opening up communication with General Gordon. It will be observed that, starting from Korti and proceeding o Gakdul and thence to Metemmeb, General Stewart's forces made a much shorter journey than by following the Nile, which from Kord runs north-east as far as Abu Ahmed, and then turns again sharply to the south, patio.; Berber to Shendy. Oa the mil) the desert route of General Stewart is shown by a heavily dotted line. His station at Gakdul is marked, the Abu Ktea Wells which were gained after the battle on Saturday week, and Shebacat Wells, between which and Metemmeh the battle took place on Monday week which has opened the way to Khartoum.
